The results show that the signal comes from halos accessible by current galaxy surveys, those that host the Lyman-break galaxies and Ly$α$ emitters at these redshifts. The luminosity-weighted bias is relatively high, with values of $4-5$.
authors: Oliver Jeong; Martin White

title: OCCAMS: A Multi-Task Learning-Based Investigation of the CMB Power Spectra
abstract: How many latent variables are needed to fit the cosmic microwave background (CMB) temperature and polarisation power spectra when a neural network is given no cosmological model, and to what extent do they map onto the standard cosmological parameters? We use multi-task learning with variational autoencoders trained on CLASS-generated spectra (TT, TE, EE) over $2\le\ell\le2500$. No cosmological model is built into the network, and the number of latent variables, $L$, is varied over $L=5$, $6$ and $7$. Their fits are compared to the Planck 2018 data using $\hatχ^2$, AIC, BIC and Bayesian evidence. Their correspondence with cosmological parameters is measured with normalised mutual information post-training. The loss weights are set within a single training run by uncertainty weighting, with the weight of the disentanglement term either fixed (semi-automated, SA) or learned (completely automated, CA). The reconstruction loss is split over multipole ranges in three configurations that separate the roles of temperature and polarisation and of the low- and high-$\ell$ ranges. In four of the six combinations of configuration and strategy, the fit improves from $L=5$ to $L=6$ and not beyond, and $L=6$ is the best, or close to the best, in five of the six cases. So, six latent variables are needed, as many as the free parameters of the standard, model-dependent approach. SA gives clearer disentanglement, while CA needs no a priori choice of the disentanglement weight and has the higher evidence at $L=5$ and $6$: the two strategies are points on a trade-off between interpretability and fit to the data. Notably, the latent variables for $τ$ and $A_s$ share almost no information in any model, consistent with large-scale polarisation separating the two, as in standard analyses. A deep-learning approach can thus give a compact, data-driven parametrisation of the CMB spectra.
authors: Ankit Mandal; Rahul Shah; Md. Wali Hossain et al.

title: UNIONS: Red and blue alignments of DESI DR1 galaxies
abstract: Intrinsic alignments (IA) of galaxies are a dominant source of systematics in weak-lensing cosmological analyses, and direct measurements on spectroscopic samples are the primary source of priors on their amplitude. We measure the IA of galaxies from the first data release (DR1) of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) as a function of colour, stellar mass, and halo mass, by cross-correlating the DESI spectroscopic catalogues with the weak-lensing shape catalogue of the Ultraviolet Near-Infrared Optical Northern Survey (UNIONS) over up to 2400 deg$^2$. We fit the three-dimensional galaxy-galaxy and galaxy-shape multipoles of the DESI BGS, LRG, and ELG samples, split by colour and stellar mass, with the non-linear linear alignment (NLA) and the tidal alignment and tidal torquing (TATT) models. Halo masses are measured for the BGS red sample from galaxy-galaxy lensing and extended to the LRGs through the resulting stellar-to-halo mass relation. Red galaxies are strongly and radially aligned, but their alignment amplitude is not a single power law of halo mass between $6\times10^{11}$ and $3\times10^{13}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$: it is nearly flat at low mass and rises steeply above a break at $1.3\times10^{13}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$. Massive blue BGS galaxies instead show a tangential alignment, detected at $3.3σ$, to our knowledge the most significant detection of a non-zero alignment of blue galaxies to date, while the low-mass blue BGS galaxies and the ELGs are consistent with zero. At our current precision, the data do not favour TATT over NLA.
authors: R. Paviot; C. Murray; M. Kilbinger et al.

title: In-depth data movement characterization of DNA read mapping algorithms
abstract: Read mapping algorithms represent a critical bottleneck in genomic analysis pipelines due to the resources required; a problem that is becoming more pronounced as sequencing technologies advance and datasets expand. We present an extensive workload characterization of leading read mapping algorithms across diverse sequencing technologies to identify hardware acceleration and optimization opportunities. We analyzed the following implementations: MashMap, wfmash, and Minimap2 for whole-genome alignment (WGA); NGMLR, Minimap2, and LRA for long reads; and Bowtie2, BWA-MEM, StrobeAlign, and minibwa for short reads. We used the Intel VTune Profiler for detailed memory analysis to identify memory- bound functions, cache usage patterns, and data transfer bottlenecks. We further analyzed a selected subset of alignment tools using the DAMOV-SIM simulator to obtain a more granular view of data movement characteristics for two different cache structures. Based on our results, Minimap2 emerges as the fastest alignment tool for long read scenarios, but falls behind in whole-genome alignment due to poor multithreading. Across all three categories, some programs (e.g., LRA, BWA-MEM) are highly memory-bound. More in-depth analysis via DAMOV-SIM revealed that some memory-bound tools, in particular, do not fully utilize the multi-level cache hierarchy in modern multi-core CPU architectures. Our results show that while some tools require algorithmic redesign for performance gains, some others can benefit from running on PIM architectures.
authors: Berkan Şahin; Ecem İlgün; Klea Zambaku et al.

title: HistoTx: Early fusion of H&E images and spatial transcriptomics at varying spatial transcriptomics resolution with self-supervised learning
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics maps gene expression across tissue sections and, when integrated with whole slide images, jointly captures both morphological architecture and molecular activity to provide a rich, multimodal view of tissue biology. ML approaches combining spatial transcriptomics and WSIs typically learn a mapping from morphological features to molecular profiles via contrastive alignment or supervised fine-tuning of pathology foundation models. In both cases, transcriptomics serves as a training signal rather than a true input modality, leaving inference fundamentally image-driven. We propose an early-fusion vision transformer architecture in which transcript tokens are constructed at arbitrary spatial resolution, merged with image patch tokens, and jointly processed through a shared transformer stack for deep cross-modal interaction. Starting from a pretrained vision-only pathology foundation model, we train HistoTx by continuing self-supervised pretraining on paired image and spatial transcriptomics data and demonstrate that: 1) at inference with image only, performance remains on par with the baseline on most tasks while improving on tasks that inherently benefit from molecular knowledge, such as gene expression prediction; 2) when both modalities are available at inference, jointly providing image and transcript inputs outperforms either modality alone.
authors: Alice Driessen; Emil Malmsten; Steffen Wolf et al.

title: Pin and Replay, or Refuse: Conditional Exactness and Probabilistic Validation Across Reference Releases
abstract: Biologists annotate genomes by searching proteins against reference databases such as Pfam, which publish new releases every few weeks to months. Each release forces a full re-search, though most of the database is unchanged: 86.6% of Pfam entries matched between releases 38.1 and 38.2 after excluding build metadata and comments. Reusing old results is hard because search programs are fixed binaries whose printed statistics depend on whole-database size. We present TARE (Tool Annotation Replay with Evidence), a wrapper that reruns an unmodified program only on entries that can matter, pinning the program's database-size setting to the new release so it prints the numbers a full run would print. TARE then tests the replay by adding back omitted entries and refuses with a failure status if any line changes, dumping a full stock body when the tool still runs. Two claims stay separate: conditional exactness under a stated contract (tested each update, not proved), and runtime assurance as probabilistic validation at a stated prevalence---not a guarantee against shipping incorrect output. In the all-record timing, TARE audits 299 records from all queries, so a hidden dependency affecting at least 1% of that population ships with probability at most 5% (valid oracle); rarer faults are outside that bound. On Pfam 38.1->38.2, TARE is 3.47x faster than a full rerun under that audit (median over 8 genomes after excluding 1 flagged genome; 95% CI 3.30-3.81). Historical candidate-population timings on the same nine genomes were 4.24x (Bernoulli; 95% CI 4.17-4.68) and 3.49x (bounded s=299; 95% CI 3.32-4.10). Cost of checking versus unchecked replay is 1.58x (C/B). Across 715,704 HMMER and Infernal output lines, none differed from a full run. TARE refused DIAMOND, whose first filter reads neighboring database bytes, and BLAST+, whose unpinned probe rows fit none of TARE's column rules.
authors: Joshua Terranova; Jiapeng Zhang

title: Evolutionary characterization of whole-genome doubling across human cancers
abstract: Whole-genome doubling (WGD) is common across human cancers and is associated with tumour progression and adverse clinical outcomes. However, how genome-doubled tumours evolve across diverse cancer types remains poorly understood. Here we characterize WGD-associated tumour evolution by integrating genomic analyses of 41,332 tumours from 12 cancer types with evolutionary timing and multi-omic data. Several canonical driver mutations generally preceded WGD when both occurred, as did the onset of homologous recombination deficiency-associated mutagenesis. Notably, post-WGD chromosome-arm losses showed substantially weaker cancer-type dependence than pre-WGD losses, with 61-75% less variance explained by cancer type. Beyond chromosomal evolution, WGD+ tumours showed reduced interferon-response and HLA antigen-presentation programmes linked to epigenetic remodelling, without disproportionate enrichment of genetic immune-escape alterations. Our findings highlight WGD as a recurrent evolutionary transition associated with altered chromosomal evolution and epigenetically linked immune adaptation across cancers.
authors: Yangyang Zhang; Haiming Li; Xiaoyu Zhao et al.

title: An auditable agentic pipeline for variant-to-gene prioritisation, validated against orthogonal functional evidence
abstract: Assigning GWAS variants to causal genes requires evidence from multiple resources. We present V2G, an agentic pipeline that records evidence retrieval and returns ranked genes alongside the retrieved evidence. We evaluate whether language-model reranking improves gene prioritisation and whether its gains depend on the retrieved evidence or recall of known associations. On 135 held-out loci where candidate retrieval succeeded and Open Targets L2G predicts, reranking by a language model improves Precision@1 over the evidence ordering it receives, 0.793 against 0.711 (+0.081, 95% CI +0.038 to +0.129), and over nearest-gene assignment (+0.178); no difference from Open Targets L2G or from training-membership baselines was detected. Given only the trait and the candidate gene symbols, in shuffled order, the same model scores 0.864 on these loci (three seeds, 0.859 - 0.867) and names the reference gene at 0.594 of the loci where the pipeline never retrieved it; with each gene's symbol moved to another gene's evidence row it follows the top-scored row and scores 0.284. The gain over the evidence ordering is recall of known genes, and the evidence as presented anchors the model to the ordering rather than informing it. Across the 296 held-out loci (five seeds each) the model keeps the given top candidate at 86% of decisions; at naturally retrieved loci its departures select a reference gene in 85% of departure decisions (31 of 37 loci), and none displaced one. Its calls carry trait-matched mouse mutant or Mendelian phenotype annotations more often than other candidates at the same locus. Train-test overlap is reported throughout. The study includes a frozen benchmark, cached predictions and reproduction code.
authors: Shakuntala Baichoo; Sohail; Sarkar et al.

title: Locality-Controlled Out-of-Distribution Guidance for Robust Regulatory DNA Sequence Design
abstract: Designing regulatory DNA sequences for targeted gene-expression control is an important challenge. Recent approaches frame this task as property-conditioned generation, where diffusion models trained on natural sequences are guided toward high predicted activity through reward-based fine-tuning or sampling-time guidance. We show that single-reward evaluation can obscure reward-hacking behavior. By decomposing evaluation into property, novelty, and plausibility, we identify an empirically underexplored region of the evaluation space in which all three objectives are satisfied, but no existing baseline succeeds. We postulate that this gap arises because prior methods treat guidance primarily as a matter of magnitude. In regulatory DNA, however, sequence grammar is spatially nonuniform: motif positions are sensitive to perturbation, while background regions allow more exploration. We therefore propose LOCOGEN by reformulating guidance as a problem of locality. LOCOGEN learns an invariant motif mask through sequence-level invariance learning to protect motif positions, while applying OOD damping only to background positions. It operates at sampling time on a frozen diffusion backbone, without retraining the backbone. Across HepG2, K562, and SK-N-SH, LOCOGEN reaches this previously underexplored region of the property-novelty-plausibility space. Code is available at https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/LocoGen.
authors: Dabin Jeong; Marwane Bourdim; Mo Lotfollahi

title: Localizing predictive concepts encoded in neural representations via hierarchical testing
abstract: Understanding which regulatory sequence motifs a genomic deep learning model has learned, with statistical error guarantees, is essential for trusting its use in downstream tasks such as variant effect prediction. Existing approaches to identifying which units in a trained network encode human- understandable concepts fall into two groups. Exploratory methods rank and visualize units but offer no statistical guarantee that the selected units are associated with the prediction target across the population of inputs. Testing-based methods test only single units or one pre-defined set of them, and do not control the error across the many sets of units. We introduce CUTTIE (Cluster-tree Unit Top-down Testing of Independence with Error control), which clusters the units of each layer into a tree and tests the clusters top-down with conditional independence tests, localizing information about the target while controlling the family-wise error rate. Thereby, we identify clusters that carry information about the target beyond the rest of the layer. For the units in the identified clusters, conditional attribution maps then reveal what motifs they encode. In a controlled simulation, the procedure identifies the clusters whose concepts affect the target. We apply the procedure to a convolutional model predicting cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility from DNA sequence, where the concepts encoded in the identified clusters map onto known regulatory motifs.
authors: Viktoriia Huryn; Marco Simnacher; Jim Berend et al.

title: Advancing Clinical Genomic Analysis with a Skill-Centred Agent
abstract: Clinical genomic analysis requires experts to integrate evolving guidelines, databases, and computational evidence. As sequencing has become increasingly accessible, this complex and labor-intensive process has become a major bottleneck to the timely use of genomic information in clinical decision-making. To fill this gap, we developed ClinGeX, a large-language-model agent that composes 105 curated executable skills through task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration. On 223 temporally held-out benchmark cases, ClinGeX achieved 71.7\% macro-averaged task-level concordance with expert reference classifications, compared with 45.7\% for the strongest comparator. In a three-condition, counterbalanced human-AI collaboration study, 45 clinical genomic professionals assessed 135 clinically derived cases under routine (no AI assistance), DeepSeek-assisted and ClinGeX-assisted conditions. ClinGeX assistance increased raw case-level concordance across criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making (51.1\%, 57.8\%, 64.4\% versus 15.6\%, 31.1\%, 20.0\% in comparator conditions) and reduced reported interpretation time in all scenarios. During an exploratory one-month real-world non-interventional assessment, 11 experienced professionals submitted feedback on 96 self-selected analysis episodes and reported frequent conclusion adoption and time savings. These findings support executable domain skills as a promising approach to augment specialist genomic interpretation.
authors: Qiaoyu Zheng; Weike Zhao; Yanjie Fan et al.

title: Evaluating and improving AI agents for sequencing protocol understanding
abstract: Existing scientific-agent benchmarks rarely evaluate whether agents can reconstruct the exact molecular structures and generation workflows specified by sequencing protocols, a capability critical for analyzing customized sequencing assays. We introduce LibStructBench, a document-grounded benchmark for reconstructing sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows. Our experiments show that frontier agents often produce approximately correct reconstructions but remain unreliable at exact reconstruction, particularly in molecular-state representation and workflow connectivity. Switching the underlying language model produced larger average performance differences than switching agent harnesses, with a statistically significant difference only for molecular-state reconstruction. Additional knowledge improved oligo-family recovery in a small pilot without improving mean molecular-workflow scores. Autonomous accumulation of procedural rules and cross-protocol examples showed non-monotonic validation performance and no mean held-out molecular-workflow improvement in the tested trajectory. These findings highlight the need for more controlled and verifiable approaches to scientific reasoning about molecular processes in complex experimental protocols.
authors: Chi-Lam Poon; Michael Goneos; Zezheng Song et al.

title: pyTransRate: reference-free quality assessment of de novo transcriptome assemblies with current aligners and quantifiers
abstract: Summary: The original software TransRate scores a de novo transcriptome assembly by mapping the reads it was built from back to it, with no reference required. Its last release (1.0.3) depends on Ruby 2.2 and on aligner and quantifier versions that can no longer be installed on most systems. pyTransRate is a Python reimplementation of the TransRate method built on snap-aligner 2.0.5 and salmon 2.7.0. In 5,031 paired comparisons (39 assembly-level metrics on each of 129 public assemblies), it reproduces the original sequence metrics and read counts exactly and ranks assemblies consistently with 1.0.3 (Spearman rho = 0.94 for assembly score, 0.98 for good-mapping rate), although its read-based scores are not numerically interchangeable with the original. It also reads gzip- and bgzip-compressed input directly. Availability and Implementation: pyTransRate is implemented in Python 3 and is freely available under the MIT license at https://github.com/macmanes-lab/pytransrate. It runs on Linux and macOS; snap-aligner and salmon are installed from Bioconda. Supplementary information: Supplementary data are available online. Supplementary Table S1 lists the assembly and read accessions for every assembly analyzed; Supplementary Table S2 gives per-assembly values from both implementations.
authors: Matthew MacManes

title: ACOR: incremental evidence accumulation towards real-time DNA storage reconstruction
abstract: DNA offers high-density, durable storage by encoding digital information into synthetic strands and retrieving it through sequencing. Sequence reconstruction combines noisy copies of each strand before downstream decoding. Conventional offline methods typically reconstruct completed read clusters, separating reconstruction from ongoing read collection. Streaming reconstruction offers a way to overlap evidence processing with sequencing and reduce the computation remaining before downstream decoding. We present ACOR, a streaming consensus reconstruction method that records $k$-mer transitions and boundary support in a persistent ledger, then decodes through length-constrained beam search and priority-based selection at cluster closure. Evaluation on real and simulated DNA-storage datasets showed competitive recovery. On our own short-read next-generation sequencing (NGS) wet-lab library, ACOR combined near-complete recovery with second-scale reconstruction of more than ten million reads. A smaller public benchmark was completed in a fraction of a second. Parallel ACOR achieved speedups of tens to over a thousand-fold relative to the tested serial baseline configurations. Sparse storage reduced high-context memory requirements, while parallel execution accelerated reconstruction computation. ACOR is designed for streaming readout pipelines that process assigned reads while sequencing continues.
authors: Linxuan Han; Huaming Wu; Shi Jia et al.

title: HELICS: Biobank-scale Conditional Synthetic Genome Generation via Latent Flow Matching
abstract: Individual-level genotype data underpin genetic discovery, disease-risk modeling, and therapeutic development, yet many critical settings remain data-limited, including underrepresented ancestries, rare or imbalanced disease cohorts, and restricted-access biobanks. Conditional synthetic genome generation would support privacy-aware benchmarking, simulation, and data augmentation, but requires learning an ultra-high-dimensional discrete distribution over hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of correlated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), or sites of DNA variation. We introduce HELICS: High-fidelity gEneration via Latent Interpolant Conditional Synthesis, a phasing-free latent flow matching framework for genome-wide SNP-level generation from biobank-scale genotype data. HELICS tokenizes chromosomes with convolutional autoencoders, reducing >600K SNPs to 4,096 continuous latent tokens, and trains a transformer parameterized conditional flow matching model over the concatenated multi-chromosome latent representation. Trained on over 417K genomes in the UK Biobank, HELICS generates genome-wide common-variant synthetic cohorts without haplotype phasing and achieves stronger fidelity to real genotypes than existing haplotype-based simulators, including high allele-frequency agreement in external evaluation and superior preservation of local and long-range SNP correlation structure. Conditioning on ancestry and genetic liability summaries enables targeted generation across genetic risk profiles; in perturbation analyses, by increasing the conditioned disease trait liability, HELICS induces SNP-level dosage changes in generated genomes that are highly correlated with published association weights. HELICS provides a scalable generative modeling framework for SNP-level genome data and a path toward conditional synthetic cohorts for data-limited genetic studies.
authors: Ahmad Abdel-Azim; Xihong Lin

title: Enhancing Clinical Classifier Robustness with Deep Representation Learning Based OOD Detection on DNA Methylation Data
abstract: DNA methylation (DNAM) array-based tumor classification is a powerful clinical diagnostic tool, but models trained on fixed reference cohorts can produce faulty predictions for tumor types not represented in the training distribution. We propose an end-to-end deep representation learning-based out-of-distribution (OOD) detection framework for DNAm array data. Deep neural network (DNN) classifiers were trained on public sarcoma (SARC) (GSE140686) and brain tumor (BT) (GSE90496) cohorts, and feature vectors were extracted from bottleneck layers. Five OOD methods, including 1dimension (1D)-Subspace Analysis (1D-SSA), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Ridge Regression, Mahalanobis Distance (MD), and Sum of Squared Distances (SSD), were explored with 200 and 500-dimensional embeddings. Spectral discrepancy was used to discriminate in-distribution (IND) from OOD samples. Performance was measured via cross-validation, holdout samples, and an independent clinical dataset. 1D-SSA was the most effective approach. In the sarcoma-IND/brain tumor-OOD setting, the framework achieved an AUROC of 0.975 and True Negative Rate (TNR)@95TPR of 0.930, and an AUROC of 0.9569 and TNR@95TPR of 0.8660 for the brain tumor-IND/sarcoma-OOD setting. On the independent clinical test set, the method yielded a mean AUROC of 0.976, a DE of 0.032, an FPR@95TPR of 0.065, and a TNR@95TPR of 0.935. These results show deep representation-based OOD detection as a practical quality-control layer for clinical-grade methylation-based tumor classification systems.
authors: Md Zahangir Alom; Quynh T. Tran; Breuer Alexandar et al.

title: Benchmarking miRNA Target Prediction Methods
abstract: Background: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate gene expression by binding to target mRNAs. Although many tools predict miRNA-target interactions, predictions show limited concordance, and benchmarks relying on curated databases may be biased by overlap with tool-development data. Methods: We benchmarked seven tools (TargetScan, miRDB, miRmap, DIANA-microT, RNA22, miRWalk, and mirDIP) across approximately 59.7 million candidate miRNA-mRNA pairs. Each pair received an evidence-graded reference score (0-3) combining validated interactions from miRTarBase and TarBase with expression-derived evidence from paired miRNA-seq and mRNA-seq data in an induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) cohort of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome and control lines. Performance was evaluated using Type I error, statistical power, and false discovery proportion (FDP). Robustness was assessed by increasing reference-score stringency (truth signal) and including progressively lower-confidence predictions (model signal). Optimal cutoffs maximized Youden's J statistic. Results: Rankings were largely consistent across settings. TargetScan and miRDB maintained Type I error rates below 0.05, with TargetScan showing the lowest FDP, but both had limited power. mirDIP achieved the highest power at the cost of the highest Type I error rate. At optimal cutoffs, mirDIP best balanced sensitivity and specificity (Youden's J = 0.566), followed by DIANA-microT (J = 0.481); miRWalk and RNA22 had FDPs near the random-prediction baseline. No tool was optimal across all metrics; tool and cutoff selection should reflect whether sensitivity or specificity is prioritized."""
authors: Congliang Jin; Weibo Niu; Zhexing Wen et al.

title: TAPESTRY: an interactive resource for exploring tumor-enriched splice junctions in pediatric brain tumors
abstract: TAPESTRY (https://tapestry.rokitalab.com) is a database and web application for exploring recurrent tumor-enriched splice junctions (TEJs) in pediatric brain tumors, cancers that carry few protein-coding mutations and therefore few mutation-derived neoantigens. However, TEJs represent a much larger source of neoantigens as potential therapeutic targets in these tumors. TAPESTRY catalogs 45,430 recurrent TEJs across 19 histologies, identified in 1,962 RNA-seq specimens (including 1,272 independent primary tumors) from the Pediatric Brain Tumor Atlas and compared to four normal brain reference cohorts comprising adult, pediatric, developmental and cell-type-resolved tissue. Each junction is classified as tumor-specific or oncofetal; annotated for splice-event type, coding consequence, novelty relative to GENCODE v39 and overlap with Pfam and UniProt protein domains; and scored for recurrence within each histology. Users can search by gene or splicing event and filter results by histology, junction class, and annotation. Users can also generate gene-level expression heatmaps across cohorts, junction-level expression boxplots, and transcript and exon diagrams, and download all tables and figures. A documented REST API supports programmatic access, and all source code is openly available. By making tumor-selective and developmentally reactivated splicing events searchable and interpretable, TAPESTRY supports the prioritization of splice-derived targets for antibody-based, cell-based and vaccine immunotherapies in pediatric brain and central nervous system tumors.
authors: Patricia J. Sullivan; Ryan J. Corbett; Chao Di et al.

title: Benchmarking Recent Single-Cell Synthetic Data Generation Methods on the OneK1K Dataset
abstract: Synthetic single-cell RNA-seq data generation offers a promising route for privacy-aware biomedical data sharing, but donor-linked datasets require careful balancing of biological utility and privacy risk. In this work, we benchmark synthetic generation methods for the CAMDA 2026 ELSA Health Privacy Challenge using the donor-split OneK1K dataset, comparing scGFT, scLDM, and Cell2Sentence across statistical fidelity, downstream biological preservation, and membership inference vulnerability. Because full-transcriptome generation is computationally demanding, we focus generative modeling on highly variable genes and evaluate alternative strategies for reconstructing non-HVG expression. Our results show that non-HVG handling is a central determinant of privacy: directly copying non-HVG values leads to severe leakage, whereas Poisson-based reconstruction substantially reduces membership inference risk. We further find that scGFT and scLDM better preserve biological structure than an independent Poisson baseline, while maintaining near-random privacy profiles under appropriate configurations. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating synthetic single-cell data beyond marginal similarity alone, emphasizing robustness, interpretability, and privacy-conscious design choices throughout preprocessing, generation, and post-processing.
authors: Buse Giledereli; Basar Temiz; Amirreza Sattarzadeh Khanehbargh

title: An autoencoder outperforms two transformers on prediction of gene expression from chromatin accessibility
abstract: Models that predict RNA abundance from chromatin accessibility are rarely compared under the same features, targets and metrics. We built one benchmark on 126,604 paired single-nucleus profiles from 19 human studies with a shared vocabulary of 50,000 peaks and 3,185 genes, ten 5x2 cross-validation folds and one scoring target, and compared seven implemented pipelines and two reference predictors across 70 trained runs; each pipeline keeps its own input normalisation and native training target. The scButterfly-B pipeline, built on dual variational autoencoders, outperformed every transformer pipeline, including an autoregressive Perceiver model (Omic Translator) and a support-free reformulation of Cisformer, on per-gene and within-cell Spearman correlation in all sixty paired fold comparisons, with 3.8 times shorter training. Transformer pipelines come within 0.02-0.04 on within-cell profile shape but lag by 0.10-0.24 on per-gene correlation. On two withheld cell types per-gene correlation is low; controls show the podocyte values are typical of within-type correlation for seen cell types of the same size, whereas Paneth values match a cell-agnostic shuffle for every Omic Translator arm. Within the transformer family, prespecified ablations show the Perceiver encoder was worth +0.0439 in within-donor per-gene correlation over full self-attention, a chromosome-aware genomic attention prior reduced it by 0.0096 (exact donor-level sign-flip test, Holm-adjusted p = 1.2e-4), and decoder output order had no detectable effect. A training-mean profile reaches 0.314 within-cell correlation with no input and a constant at the true expressed-gene positions reaches 0.996 per-gene correlation, so oracle-support protocols are reported only as diagnostics. Code, results and an audited release are provided.
authors: Jesse G. Meyer

title: BARRR: Bidimensional Augmented Reduced Rank Regression for Multi-View Multi-Cohort Data
abstract: Bidimensional data integration across multiple cohorts (i.e., sample groups) and views (i.e., sources or modalities) is crucial in biomedical research to derive holistic insights from heterogeneous datasets. However, most existing integrative methods focus on a single dimension, such as multi-view integration across distinct sources or multi-cohort integration across distinct sample groups. Existing approaches for bidimensional integration are scarce and predominantly unsupervised, overlooking the valuable insights offered by covariates. To address this gap, we introduce the Bidimensional Augmented Reduced Rank Regression (baRRR) method. Our approach models covariate-related and unrelated effects concurrently, while also decomposing effect levels (global, partially shared, and individual) across both dimensions. Extensive simulations demonstrate the advantages of our method with respect to signal recovery, outcome prediction, and missing data imputation. We apply our approach to data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), using somatic mutations as covariates to inform patterns of variability across different omics platforms and cancer types. These studies highlight its potential as a robust and adaptable tool for integrative analysis in biomedical research.
authors: Jiuzhou Wang; Eric F. Lock

title: Reading Between the Reads: A Decade On, Revisiting Sequencing Protocol Annotation in the Sequence Read Archive
abstract: Background: Experimental metadata are essential for interpreting archived sequencing data. In 2015, Alnasir and Shanahan examined the annotation of fragmentation, adapter ligation and enrichment in the Sequence Read Archive (SRA). This study revisits those measurements using the original SQL keyword definitions on a September 2026 NCBI metadata snapshot reconstructed in the historical SRAdb schema. Results: The contemporary database contained 41,593,302 experiments, compared with 419,620 in 2013. In library_construction_protocol, the proportion matching all three historical keyword groups declined from 4.06% to 1.42%. The protocol field was NULL in 67.65% of contemporary experiments. Searching design_description alongside the protocol field increased combined three-step keyword detection to 1,197,367 experiments (2.88%), with most additional matches occurring where the protocol field was NULL. Coverage varied across sequencing library strategies, ranging from 0.26% for AMPLICON to 7.69% for RNA-Seq. Independent comparison of 150 sampled experiment records against source XML confirmed agreement in all historical keyword classifications. Conclusions: The original criteria identify a smaller proportion of experiments in the designated protocol field than a decade earlier. Additional preparation-related terminology is detectable in general experiment descriptions, exposing the limitations of searches restricted to one metadata field. Differences among sequencing strategies complicate historical comparisons as preparation methods evolve. The findings support more consistent protocol annotation and the need to distinguish keyword occurrence from the adequacy of experimental documentation.
authors: Jamie J. Alnasir

title: HyperTaxa: Multiscale Genome Representations for Generalized Microbial Taxonomic Inference
abstract: Reliable microbial taxonomic inference is challenged by the rapid growth of newly sequenced organisms and incomplete reference coverage. While alignment- and database-driven tools remain essential for reference-backed identification, they are not designed for learned inference over species absent from genome-level training. We introduce HyperTaxa, a taxonomy-aligned representation learning framework for open-set microbial taxonomic inference. HyperTaxa encodes whole genomes as multiscale hyperspectral k-mer transition fields and aligns these representations to a taxonomy-derived semantic space using a two-stage Node2Vec-to-MDS procedure that combines local graph structure with global hierarchical distance preservation. The resulting space supports zero-shot inference over species excluded from genome-level training but represented in the taxonomy, generalized zero-shot inference over seen and unseen species, and cascaded genus-to-species prediction. Across benchmark and large-scale disjoint-species evaluations, HyperTaxa improves taxonomic prediction over pseudo-image and transformer-graph baselines, with the strongest gains at higher taxonomic ranks. Ablations further show that multiscale transition encoding and taxonomy-aware alignment are key contributors to generalization. These results position HyperTaxa as a complementary taxonomy-aware representation and candidate-generation framework for microbial identification under incomplete reference coverage and open-set uncertainty.
authors: Akash Rao; Sushim Gupta; Vishalini Ramnath et al.

title: panvram: GPU-resident random access to a human pangenome cohort
abstract: Repeatedly sampling short sequence windows from a human pangenome requires an access representation as well as compression. panvram stores each assembly as a reference-relative block archive and pools these archives on a GPU. For 558 haplotype assemblies, the default q4k representation occupies 16.642 GB of persistent pools including the decoded reference; a packed-reference, compact-directory representation occupies 11.634 GB. These quantities are not peak application memory. In the C1 experiment, default and fully compact forms delivered 743,271 and 736,762 windows/s; a separate public Colab run delivered 741,931 and 680,760 windows/s. All are batch API measurements and must not be pooled as repeated trials of an identical environment. Full-decoding checks compared reconstructed FASTA checksums with the manifest. On the CPU, the M6 shuffled-window workload at the same cohort cardinality reported 26 requests/s for AGC and 145,222 requests/s for refrel3 q4k. This comparison concerns one-thread requests of 4 KiB on the recorded warm-cache workload, not all genome-access patterns. AGC provides the smaller incremental archive: 5.40 MB/assembly versus 13.04 MB/assembly for refrel3 q16k, with different exclusions; the size pair is not the same refrel3 configuration as the q4k timing pair. We derive an expected-work expression for fixed independent granules and distinguish it from an empirical median-latency predictor. Cohort-scale counter and DRAM measurements motivate a locality hypothesis, but do not establish a causal per-miss latency or independently reproduce a model-failure verdict. The window-cost verdict at N=558 is published with its harness and raw timings.
authors: Yakiv Shavidze

title: Reducing double-dipping in single-cell topic models with three-way count splitting
abstract: Topic models learn gene programs from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data, and the same counts are then used to test which genes and donors are associated with those programs. Count splitting is the standard remedy for this reuse, but it has not been tested when an encoder reads each cell's counts. On a 104,400-cell lupus cohort with 300 permuted null genes per run, naive tests rejected 36% of null gene-topic pairs at a nominal 5% level, and the usual two-way split rejected 38%, because the encoder sees the tested gene's own held-out count. Encoding topic usage on a separate third of the counts, with beta-binomial thinning, lowered this to 7.7% (6.7% for genes outside the model); for two other models, LDVAE and scETM, the rate was 7.0-7.3% (naive 51-59%). A label-free interferon program shifts in held-out counts in the lupus cohort and in a pre-specified COVID-19 cohort, and donor-level topic usage predicts disease (AUROC 0.96) beyond cell-type proportions (0.86 and 0.58 in the two cohorts). Calibration and prediction did not depend on the model. We do not claim better clustering, prediction or topic stability. Code, figures and result tables are public (MIT license; DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23307193).
authors: Zheng Qu

title: Harness-Driven Agentic Operation of Optical Pooled Screen Analysis
abstract: Optical pooled screens connect genetic perturbations to changes in cell morphology and behavior, but turning the microscopy data into interpretable results takes complex, multi-day analyses. Established pipelines process this data, yet researchers still select parameters, inspect outputs, and resolve failures for each experiment. Here, we present Brieflow-auto, a pipeline-specific harness implemented as a Claude Code plugin that lets a coding large language model (LLM) operate Brieflow, an open-source end-to-end pipeline for optical pooled screening data. A researcher supplies experimental facts and approves the launch. An agent tunes parameters in an interactive notebook, and the harness validates the configuration, monitors execution, recovers from common failures, and checks output quality. For pipeline defects, the agent opens upstream issues proposing backward-compatible fixes for the broader community. In five previously analyzed screens, harness runs yielded more cells with a confident single-gene assignment than the original hand analyses. On a screen the pipeline was not designed for, the harness turned each failure into a reviewed upstream fix. More broadly, we propose that wrapping an established pipeline in a harness can substantially accelerate its use and the long-term reliability of its codebase.
authors: Matteo Di Bernardo; Claire Peterson; Ege Topkoc et al.

title: Panoramic modelling of single-cell transcriptomes at scale with CellNet
abstract: Comprehensively characterizing cellular landscapes to elucidate cell diversity is a central goal in biology. Recent advances in single-cell profiling have created unprecedented opportunities for this endeavor by capturing diverse transcriptomes with remarkable breadth. However, current foundation models generally struggle to leverage such holistic and valuable information to represent a cell. Here we present CellNet, which enables panoramic modelling of single-cell transcriptomes at scale by integrating DNA-derived gene identities and measured RNA expression into a shared image representation. Pretrained on 231 million image-based cell profiles across 40 species and covering over one million genes, CellNet improves the recognition of rare and condition-associated cellular states, enables the study of genes beyond experimentally measured panels, and uncovers associations between poorly characterized non-coding RNAs and known biological programmes. CellNet paves the way for AI-enabled cell-biology discovery at the whole-transcriptome scale. The CellNet website is available at https://www.cellnet.top.
authors: Xiaoqing Lian; Pei Liu; Jiahui Tan et al.

title: OmicsBench: a long-horizon multi-turn benchmark of AI agents on research-study-scale bioinformatics
abstract: Computational biologists increasingly delegate substantial analyses to AI agents in long-horizon, multi-turn sessions, yet most benchmarks of agents' bioinformatics capabilities pose a single short task with a single-shot prompt. We present OmicsBench, a long-horizon, multi-turn bioinformatics benchmark for AI agents. Each of its 97 tasks links dependent subtasks into a directed acyclic graph, for 662 underlying subtasks in all. Each subtask is posed as one user turn and graded deterministically against an answer key, with optional in-context feedback on incorrect answers. Across 12 models on three harnesses, the slowest agent averages 3.6 hours per task, and no combination comes near saturating the benchmark, with mean scores of 0.43 to 0.57 out of a possible 1 without in-context feedback and 0.54 to 0.67 with it. Multi-turn evaluation also uncovers behavior that single-shot prompts cannot, as agents score lower on subtasks that depend on earlier subtasks, and in-context feedback helps agents recover some of that loss. Because deterministic scoring gives no qualitative account of how an agent failed, we also introduce an unsupervised failure mode discovery pipeline that describes, embeds, and clusters agents' failed attempts to surface emergent failure modes. Applied to OmicsBench, this pipeline exposes qualitative shortcomings in how agents carry out bioinformatics analyses, ranging from agents applying their own statistical filters in place of the specified ones to agents writing whole answers from memory.
authors: Gideon Shaked; Siddharth Nagisetty

title: Deep learning-based virtual perturbation reveals increasing heterogeneity of gene regulatory responses with aging
abstract: A central hypothesis in aging biology proposes that the gradual accumulation of stochastic molecular damage drives transcriptional deregulation (TD), ultimately leading to functional decline. However, existing single-cell analyses largely rely on static expression measurements and provide limited resolution of how regulatory responses change at the level of individual cells. Here, we leverage DKO, a deep learning framework that predicts cell-specific virtual gene perturbation effects from unperturbed transcriptomes, capturing cell-to-cell differences in regulatory context without requiring a reconstructed gene regulatory network or matched perturbation data. Applying DKO to single-cell transcriptomic datasets from humans, mice, Drosophila, and C. elegans revealed that the transcriptional consequences of perturbing the same gene became increasingly heterogeneous across cells with age, indicating that gene regulatory responses become less consistent and more dependent on cellular context. Furthermore, we find that cells with higher somatic mutation burdens have greater knockout-response variability, linking accumulated molecular damage to regulatory inconsistency. Within the same cellular populations, higher impact variability was also associated with higher senescence scores, linking transcriptional dysregulation to senescence-associated states. Our findings identify a progressive loss of regulatory robustness at both the gene and cell levels as a conserved feature of aging, linking stochastic molecular damage to increasing heterogeneity in cellular regulatory responses.
authors: Yongjian He; Julia Hanna Haddad Guez; Xu-Wen Wang et al.

title: VitisGP: Multi-Task Benchmark for Genotype to Phenotype Grapevine Prediction
abstract: As climate change reshapes grape-growing conditions, predicting grapevine phenotypes from genomic variation is increasingly important for identifying and breeding cultivars suited to emerging environmental pressures. Existing research on the grapevine genotype-phenotype relationship using machine learning has often focused on individual traits, isolated regions, or a limited set of predictive models. We introduce VitisGP, a multi-phenotype curated dataset, integrating genome-wide SNP data with 26 heterogeneous phenotype prediction tasks spanning sommelier-curated aroma traits (N=11), botanical traits (N=14) and wine color---across 1,197 Vitis vinifera cultivars. We employ VitisGP to benchmark phenotype prediction, comparing machine-learning models with differing inductive biases---L2-regularized logistic regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, GBLUP and Transformer-based models, providing the first systematic comparison of this breadth on harmonized grapevine data. Across the benchmark, CatBoost achieves the strongest overall performance (macro-average AUROC=0.696 across 26 tasks), although model performance varies substantially across phenotype classes, with sensory and color traits showing stronger predictability than agronomic characteristics. VitisGP provides the community with a resource for investigating the genomic basis of phenotypic traits and screening grapevine diversity for climate-relevant characteristics.
authors: Chiara D'Ercoli; May Levin; Pietro Liò

title: Spatial Kernel Restricted Canonical Correlation Analysis: Population Targets, Identifiability, and Stability
abstract: Relating observations of different categories across space requires methods that accommodate distinct sampling locations and spatial dependence. Spatial kernel restricted canonical correlation analysis (skrCCA) uses spatial weights to identify associated feature combinations across data categories. Here, we develop a statistical theory of its covariance form after feature reduction. Conditional on the observed locations and under a mean-zero model, the pairwise association matrices target kernel-weighted averages of cross-covariances. For prespecified directions, we derive the exact null variance under independence between blocks. We establish recovery and stability bounds in two- and multiblock settings under explicit population models, and show that exact cyclic updates have convergent objective values. The variance characterization shows how spatial weighting and within-block dependence jointly determine the effective information available for estimating association. The recovery bounds separate statistical and optimization error, relating stability to population separation and the strength of connections between blocks. These results clarify what fitted spatial association axes estimate and provide conditions under which they can be recovered reliably.
authors: Zhen Miao; Yilong Qu; Nancy R. Zhang

title: Understanding Gene Expression-to-Image Learning: Spatial Structure and Information Fidelity
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables cell-level analysis of biological heterogeneity, but learning effective representations from high-dimensional, unordered gene expression profiles remains challenging. Gene Expression-to-Image (GE2I) offers an effective learning strategy by arranging gene values on pixel grids for convolutional neural networks, but its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We study GE2I on full-transcriptome data while keeping the network and training procedure fixed. Our results reveal a trade-off between spatial smoothness and gene-level fidelity. Structured mappings produce smooth, low-frequency patterns that support faster early optimization, whereas assigning multiple genes to the same pixel obscures expression differences and can reduce predictive performance. This trade-off explains why random mappings can compete with structured layouts when many genes are represented. One-to-one gene-to-pixel assignment improves prediction across the tested visual backbones even when image smoothness decreases. We further find that the benefits of pretraining and augmentation depend on the backbone and mapping. These findings provide practical guidance for pixel allocation and the transfer of vision priors to gene expression data.
authors: Xiaoqing Lian; Pei Liu; Jiahui Tan et al.

title: CellChain: Benchmarking Cross-Scale Evidence Use for Perturbation Reasoning
abstract: Recent advances in foundation models and large-scale cellular perturbation datasets have driven growing interest in using LLMs to predict and reason about cellular responses. Biological reasoning in this setting involves relating molecular mechanisms, cellular responses, and functional outcomes across scales. Evaluating foundation models therefore requires assessing not only whether their predictions are correct, but also how those predictions depend on the biological evidence provided. We introduce CellChain, an experimentally grounded benchmark comprising 590 biological cases and 2,360 matched evidence-condition instances across gene-dependency prediction, cytokine-axis identification, and drug-sensitivity ranking. CellChain links perturbation experiments and external biological resources through a provenance-aware evidence graph spanning molecular, pathway, transcriptional, and phenotypic information. Task-specific conditions vary evidence coverage, composition, or assignment while preserving questions, candidate answers, reference targets, and scoring rules. Across 18 foundation models, the highest accuracies under prespecified target-evidence conditions are 57.5%, 75.5%, and 70.8%, respectively, and broader evidence coverage does not consistently improve accuracy. On the drug-sensitivity benchmark cohort, matched reference histories outperform swapped histories by an average of 13.0 percentage points in cluster-weighted accuracy. Decision-transition analysis separates corrections, newly introduced errors, and wrong-answer switches, revealing substantial answer changes hidden by small net accuracy differences. CellChain provides controlled comparisons for attributing changes in model predictions to prespecified expansions of biological context, including changes in evidence coverage, composition, and biological assignment.
authors: Xue Xia; Yue Wang; Shuizhou Chen et al.

title: Tree-based Algorithms for Breakpoint Median and Near-Median Genomes
abstract: Median genomes serve as candidates for ancestral reconstruction and help study the diversity of parsimonious rearrangement solutions. However, the breakpoint median problem is NP-hard for unichromosomal genomes, and medians are non-unique, making their diversity important to study. In this paper, we develop tree-based algorithms for studying breakpoint medians of linear unichromosomal genomes represented as unsigned permutations. The algorithms construct rooted labeled trees whose leaves encode candidate median genomes satisfying local adjacency constraints derived from the inputs. We show that the resulting reduced search spaces contain all breakpoint medians while being much smaller than the full permutation space. We investigate these reduced spaces experimentally for three-genome instances. Our method finds exact medians and many near-optimal approximations, while early sampling of leaves often produces near-medians quickly. We also introduce constrained sampling procedures for targeting balanced near-medians, whose distances to the input genomes are more evenly distributed and hence are particularly relevant for ancestral reconstruction. The resulting framework provides a unified method for exact enumeration, efficient sampling, and targeted exploration of median and near-median genomes. In contrast to Traveling Salesman Problem-based approaches, which typically return a single solution and do not reveal the diversity or balance of the median set, our method can enumerate all medians, sample near-medians early, and target structurally distinct candidates under the breakpoint distance.
authors: Poly H. da Silva; Arash Jamshidpey; David Sankoff

title: CloneOT: predicting clone-specific perturbation responses with lineage-supervised neural inverse optimal transport
abstract: Predicting single-cell perturbation responses requires mapping between two unpaired populations of cells measured before and after the perturbation. Optimal transport (OT) provides a principled framework for constructing such mappings by minimizing the transport cost, and neural OT methods (\textit{e.g.}, CellOT) have been employed for this prediction task. However, these methods rely on a fixed transport cost, typically the squared Euclidean distance. This cost may connect cells with the wrong responses. Lineage tracing provides the information needed to learn the cost, as heritable barcodes link the cells of the same clone before and after the perturbation. Here, we propose \CloneOT, a neural inverse OT method that learns both the transport cost and the transport map from partially lineage-traced single-cell datasets. \CloneOT\ represents the cost as a neural network. It learns the cost by minimizing the extra cost that the lineage adds to the optimal transport, so that the cheapest transport keeps the cells of each clone together. Our experiments demonstrate that \CloneOT\ recovers the correct transport on 2D datasets, while the squared Euclidean cost fails. Moreover, \CloneOT\ outperforms five baselines on 14 lineage-tracing perturbation scenarios of cancer cells, for both seen and unseen clones. Furthermore, we show that \CloneOT\ reveals the clone-specific transcriptional programs of drug-tolerant persister cells and forecasts the fate of each clone from its cells before treatment. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/CloneOT.
authors: Yanshuo Chen; Wei Chen; Heng Huang

title: Training-Data Extraction from Genomic Language Models
abstract: Genomic language models generate long nucleotide continuations from short prefixes, exposing a direct route for studying training-sequence extraction through the generation interface. We present an output-only black-box attack on Evo 2 that selects convergent groups of repeated generations without gradients, token likelihoods, or training-corpus access during candidate selection. Recovered content is then scored by an evaluator combining aligned length, nucleotide identity, match multiplicity, and sequence complexity. Across 304 runs on Evo 2 7B with bacteriophage and plasmid prefixes, the attack yields 888 candidate clusters, of which 85 match training segments of at least 500 bp, giving a cluster-level attack success rate of 9.57%. Final filtering retains 22 uniquely matched extraction events at the 500-bp threshold and 15 at 1,000 bp, covering 14 and 7 distinct training-sequence regions, respectively. Within-category source-homology screening retains 11 of the 22 events at a 99% exclusion threshold and four at 98%, with the latter mapping to two reference regions. The results establish convergence among repeated nucleotide generations as a practical output-only signal for recovering long training-sequence segments and characterize how recovery depends on prefix length, cluster size, perplexity, early stopping, and sequence domains.
authors: Tianhao Mao; Zihao Wang; Dongfang Zhao et al.

title: Homogeneity and heterogeneity of functional element composition of genome units across human and seven model organisms
abstract: Is a chromosome a miniature of its genome, with the same mix of functional elements as the whole? We ask this of eight annotated genomes: human, mouse, zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Arabidopsis thaliana and maize. Elements are classified in a four-level hierarchy, from five major classes (protein-coding genes, ncRNA genes, transposable elements (TEs), pseudogenes, IG/TR gene segments) down to finer classes. Units are chromosomes or arms, cytogenetic bands, equal cuts of each chromosome, and random segments of matching size. We compare each unit with the genome and with other units, call compositions homogeneous when they differ by less than 5%, and score each against a random sample of the same size. The first finding is a surprising homogeneity. The level-1 compositions of the major chromosomes match each other and the genome in maize, zebrafish, yeast and C. elegans, and in fly down to the major arms. Finer classes can be homogeneous too: protein function in Arabidopsis, and the Wicker TE orders in maize. Enzyme reaction classes are interchangeable between chromosomes in all eight genomes. The second finding is a structured heterogeneity. Where a unit departs from its genome, it does so in one of three ways: clusters of named elements, such as rRNA genes or immune receptor loci; megabase-scale compartments, such as TE-rich pericentromeric heterochromatin; and lineage-specific gene families, visible only at the finest levels. Corrected for chance, the genomes fall into groups. For protein function and gene families, composition is more uniform in plants and fly than in vertebrates, and least uniform in C. elegans. For the major classes and TE orders, uniformity follows where each genome places its repeats, along the arms (maize, zebrafish) or around the centromeres (Arabidopsis, fly), not its lineage.
authors: Yanying Wu

title: manylp: reproducible, exact, and batched linear programming for genome-scale dynamic flux balance analysis
abstract: Dynamic flux balance analysis (dFBA) and its community, spatial and ensemble variants predict microbial metabolism by solving one linear program (LP) per species and time step, often 10^6 to 10^8 LPs per study. These LPs share their constraint matrix and objective and differ only in their bounds, yet general-purpose solvers treat each one independently, and GPU first-order solvers struggle with the degenerate, badly scaled matrices of genome-scale models. Moreover, metabolic optima are usually faces rather than vertices, so solvers return arbitrary flux vectors and dFBA predictions depend on the solver used. We present manylp, a batched solver for such bounds-parametric LP families that returns certified vertex solutions. Building on the bunching technique of stochastic programming, manylp caches optimal bases and certifies whole batches with one dense matrix product per basis on CPUs or GPUs; LPs outside the cached critical regions are re-solved by a warm-started lexicographic dual simplex, and new bases are propagated across the batch. Each LP is certified optimal and unique under a lexicographic flux rule, or infeasible, in independent double-precision arithmetic. On a genome-scale dFBA workload, manylp certified 47,889 LPs per second on a CPU, 12 to 33 times faster than HiGHS, Gurobi, FICO Xpress, GLPK and OR-Tools (32 processes), and reached 682,000 LPs per second on one GPU for community ensembles, needing 76 simplex solves for 94.6 million LPs. Integrated into the muODE simulator, it accelerated single trajectories 84-fold and 16-member ensembles 635-fold, and made adaptive Runge-Kutta integration affordable, reducing biomass errors 83-fold. Integrating 49 equally optimal flux policies in one batched run showed that alternative optima change predicted acetate 4.2-fold and shift community composition. manylp is open source: https://github.com/cumbof/manylp.
authors: Fabio Cumbo

title: Double-Take: Improving Capacity, Binding, and Selectivity In Long-Context Within Bidirectional Memory
abstract: Processing a long sequence does not guarantee that distant information remains usable. As context grows, a fixed-size memory must retain many associations, connect information across positions, and preserve relevant structure without being overwhelmed by everything it observes. These are distinct requirements: a memory may store more information without representing the relationships needed for retrieval, and it may transport those relationships without preserving the ones that matter. Thus, the challenge is not simply extending context length, but constructing a memory that remains usable as context grows. We study this problem in large-chunk test-time training (TTT) and identify two basic failures: single-step writes accumulate interference, limiting capacity, while self-associative writes cannot form cross-position bindings. We introduce Double-Take (DT), which repairs these failures with multi-step unpinned updates and cross-position mixing, and adds bidirectional change-sensitive writes for selective retention. Capacity alone leaves end-to-end recall at the $0.10$ chance floor; adding binding raises it to $0.92$. Trained only on $32\,\mathrm{kb}$ genomic contexts, DT reaches $0.927$ AUROC at $131\,\mathrm{kb}$ and $0.856$ near $1\,\mathrm{Mb}$, while transferring zero-shot from human to mouse. Together, these results identify capacity, binding, and selectivity as three requirements for usable long-range memory.
authors: Vakul Raghavan; Utkarsh Grover; Mingyang Mao et al.

title: Unlocking the Regulatory Genome by ARGUS: An Evidence-Constrained Agentic Framework for Interpreting Single Nucleotide Variants
abstract: Over 90% of disease-associated variants from genome-wide association studies fall in noncoding regulatory regions, yet their functional interpretation remains a central open problem in genomic medicine. Large language models prompted to interpret such variants routinely hallucinate transcription factor (TF) binding changes, fabricate experimental support, and assign biological significance to statistically negligible signals. We present ARGUS (Agentic Regulatory Genomics for an Uncertainty-aware Scientist), which strictly separates deterministic biological computation from LLM-mediated reasoning. ARGUS wraps 458 DNABERT-based TF binding models in a hypothesis-directed investigation loop where a planner selects evidence sources based on current uncertainty, a verifier deterministically interprets each observation, and intermediate results change the investigation path. On variant rs6983267 at the 8q24 cancer risk locus, the same planner produces four divergent trajectories for four TFs. FOXA1 is rescued in 3 steps when real ADASTRA allele-specific binding data (15 experiments, FDR = 0.030) reveals a model false negative masked by saturation. KLF6 traverses 8 steps across ADASTRA, JASPAR motif analysis, and ENCODE cCRE regulatory annotation before abstaining due to mixed indirect evidence. RAD21 abstains in 8 steps after ADASTRA returns a coverage-qualified but nonsignificant allelic test (5 experiments, FDR = 0.65), and SP1, which shares FOXA1's saturated retained prediction, abstains because no direct experimental evidence exists at this locus. All observations come from real ADASTRA, JASPAR, and ENCODE cCRE queries; none are simulated. A comparison of fixed-priority and LLM-mediated planning shows that the LLM planner reaches identical verdicts with fewer tool calls by declining evidence that cannot resolve the claim under test.
authors: Pratik Dutta; Matthew B. Obusan; Max Chao et al.

title: Predictive Multiplicity in Cell-Fate Assignment: Label-Free Rashomon Sets and the Limits of Per-Cell Certification
abstract: Single-cell trajectory inference maps transcriptomic measurements onto developmental continua, yet configurations that fit the data equally well can assign conflicting cell fates. FateMultiplicity is a label-free framework that constructs a statistically admissible model set, or Rashomon set, without lineage labels, by evaluating model discrepancy on cross-fitted held-out genes under non-inferiority testing calibrated against random-seed variation. Multiplicity is large and depends more on the diversity of the model space than its size: twelve configurations of a second algorithm expose 20.0% of cells where twenty-four of the first expose 3.8%. Whether the per-cell certified fate margin FM yields more reliable assignments than the fitted model already provides is then tested, and it does not. On simulation ground truth, on the same cells, FM discriminates misassignment at AUC 0.682, against 0.965 for the baseline configuration's own decision margin (p = 0.003) and 0.854 for a seed-dispersion baseline. Informativeness is governed by the breadth of the admitted set, not its cardinality: at cardinality four, seed refits give 0.933 and hyperparameter-perturbed sets 0.701. Relaxing the infimum to a q-quantile recovers discrimination but converges toward the single model's own confidence; the supremum reaches 0.973 because theta*'s membership bounds it from below, while the infimum is unanchored. Multiplicity in trajectory inference is worth measuring and reporting, but per-cell certification over a label-free Rashomon set is not a route to more reliable fate calls. Two constructions survive: a margin-erosion ratio separates real from spurious branch points in simulation (AUC 0.890, untested on real data), and against clonally observed fate, uncertified cells disagree with their clone's outcome 16.4 percentage points more often than certified cells (p < 0.001).
authors: Arjun Bhupatiraju; Abhiram Bhupatiraju

title: Cohort Effects, Not Treatment Response, Dominate Public Immunotherapy Cohorts: Evidence from Microbiome and Tumor Genomic Data
abstract: Researchers often pool public gut microbiome datasets from immunotherapy studies to get around small sample sizes, assuming that adding cohorts adds statistical power faster than it adds differences between studies. We test that assumption. We processed four public shotgun metagenomic cohorts of patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade through one pipeline and pooled them step by step, from 39 to 283 patients. Because the PERMANOVA effect size R^2 is above zero even when there is no real effect, we compared every result with its exact chance expectation. Measured as raw variance explained, cohort membership accounted for 8 to 27 times more variance than treatment response, although much of that ratio comes from sample size alone. At every pooling step, treatment response explained no more variance than chance (within 0.2 percentage points) and was never significant, while cohort membership explained 6.0 to 9.5 percentage points beyond chance (p = 0.001 each time). Classification stayed at chance across three model types, none of six leak-free batch-correction strategies recovered signal, and no genus reached significance in a random-effects meta-analysis. The largest single cohort (n = 165) was also non-significant, although simulation shows it had at least 90% power to detect an effect at its own 95% upper bound; within it, recruiting site alone explained 7.0 percentage points beyond chance. In three tumor genomic cohorts (n = 223), a small but real response effect sat next to a cohort effect about eighteen times larger, so the problem is not specific to microbiome data. We release batch_detector, an open tool that reports chance-corrected cohort and response effects before pooling, and test it on an independent colorectal cancer meta-analysis.
authors: Amey Garg

title: RADAgent: Automating RADseq Pipelines with Private Open-Source LLMs
abstract: Restriction site-associated DNA sequencing (RADseq) is a family of reduced-representation sequencing methods. It uses restriction enzymes to sample subsets of the genome, therefore allowing multiple individuals to be sequenced and genotyped together at low cost. RADseq is widely used for population genomics, evolutionary biology, marker discovery, and the development of SNP panels, but complete analysis still requires expert coordination across multiple tools and processing stages. Traditional RADseq analysis requires expert coordination of heterogeneous bioinformatics tools, intermediate artifacts, quality-control checks, and parameter-dependent decisions across multiple stages. Although individual steps can be scripted, executing the complete workflow still requires human oversight for state tracking, result validation, and failure handling. To automate this expert-driven coordination, we present RADAgent, which introduces a modular agentic method for reliable RADseq workflow execution with an open-weight LLM. RADAgent maps the natural boundaries of the RADseq workflow into 16 independently executable and verifiable agent modules and uses a model-independent runtime for bounded tool execution, on-disk verification, and failure recovery. We evaluate RADAgent on a real population-genomics dataset containing 476 samples from 19 populations. The results demonstrate that RADAgent reliably automates the complete RADseq workflow with an open-weight LLM while keeping genomic data and model execution within the local computing environment. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/wenlu-lab/RADAgent.
authors: Qiming Guo; Malaka Sudhakara Bava Sukruth Reddy; Honggang Zhao et al.

title: Taxonomic Classification with Tag Arrays
abstract: Taxonomic classifiers based on exact matches differ in which matches they use and in how each match splits its credit among the taxa containing it: Kraken~2 gives a $k$-mer's credit to the lowest common ancestor of those taxa, SPUMONI~2 labels each position of the read, Tagger gives each maximal exact match (MEM) one label, and Cliffy splits a match's credit evenly over a roughly logarithmic sample of the taxa. We compare these schemes on the same long MEMs, mainly on short 16S rRNA reads classified to genera with SILVA, where credit proportional to the number of occurrences of the MEM in each taxon is the most accurate, by 1.0 to 6.8 percentage points. We compute long MEMs with Boyer--Moore--Li on a run-length compressed suffix array, and count their occurrences in each taxon with a complete, run-length compressed tag array, in time proportional to the number of tag runs in the MEM's BWT interval, without locating any occurrence. We bound the number of tag runs in terms of the BWT runs and of how often suffixes with long common prefixes have different tags, and show that tags constant on $d$ blocks of the text have a macro scheme with at most $r + 2d$ phrases. On SILVA our index takes 1.44\,GB and classifies a read in 66\,$μ$s with one thread at 93.8\% accuracy; on the same reads and server, it is 14 times smaller than Cliffy's undigested index, and 4.4 times faster and 8 percentage points more accurate than Cliffy's LCA query on it. Over minimizer digests it takes 0.49\,GB and reaches 92.5\%; on the server, 92.1\% against 84.2\% for Cliffy's LCA query on its digested index. On nanopore reads from whole genomes, where almost every long MEM occurs in one species, we instead use each read's longest MEMs, found in one pass of a variant of Boyer--Moore--Li with a $k$-mer filter, which assigns 99.6\% of the reads to their species with no length threshold.
authors: Travis Gagie; Gonzalo Navarro

title: Truecell reproduces R Seurat's single-cell analysis outputs natively in the Python ecosystem
abstract: Single-cell RNA-sequencing analyses predominantly use either Seurat (R) or Scanpy (Python), with the choice often driven by programming language preference. However, by default, these tools produce divergent variable features, neighbour graphs, clusters, and marker genes. Laboratories requiring Python, which supports most deep-learning, foundation-model, and agent tools, must re-implement Seurat analyses in a framework that does not replicate Seurat's results. Truecell was developed as a Python implementation of the Seurat interface, preserving function names, arguments, default settings, and the object model to facilitate seamless transfer of analyses. In eighteen paired end-to-end evaluations against R Seurat, deterministic outputs matched to floating-point precision, and fold-change order was identical across all nine differential expression tests. In a three-arm benchmark on three datasets, with fixed user parameters and 20 seeds per tool, Truecell more closely reproduced Seurat's clustering than a Seurat-configured Scanpy in all 12 combinations of dataset and resolution settings. Truecell's marker genes and enriched pathways were also closer to Seurat's than Scanpy's were, and pseudobulk DESeq2 reproduced Seurat's gene lists with a Jaccard index ranging from 0.95 to 1.00. This agreement reflects fidelity to Seurat rather than biological correctness.
authors: Nuzla Ismail; Shanika Amarasoma; Michelle Galeas-Pena et al.

title: Beyond the Transcriptome: Chromatin-Informed Prediction of Cell-State-Dependent Perturbation Responses
abstract: Predicting transcriptional responses to genetic perturbations is central to understanding gene function. Existing predictors primarily rely on transcriptomic measurements, although chromatin accessibility provides complementary information about the cellular context in which perturbations act. Using this information requires linking chromatin context to specific perturbations and accounting for baseline differences between independently sampled control and perturbed populations. We propose ChromaPert, a chromatin-informed framework for predicting state-dependent perturbation responses. ChromaPert combines molecular and DNA-informed locus priors with paired control RNA--ATAC features to jointly represent target identity and measured cellular context. Its Chromatin-Guided Response Router (CGRR) builds a source bank of control-derived expression offsets and retrieves relevant sources using perturbation/locus or control-ATAC similarity. These offsets account for baseline differences, while conditional transport flow learns the remaining response. Across three unseen-target and held-out-state settings on K562 CAT-ATAC and Perturb-Multiome, ChromaPert achieves the highest all-gene response correlation among evaluated methods. When transferring known perturbations to held-out states, it improves correlation by 23.2% across all genes and 46.2% for the twenty most responsive genes over the strongest respective baselines. Correct RNA--ATAC pairing improves recovery of chromatin-associated response slopes over shuffled pairing, while cross-state predictions retain state-specific responses to the same perturbation.
authors: Jiafa Ruan; Chenyang He; Ruijie Quan et al.

title: HRPv2: an automated and enhanced method for full-length homology-based R-gene prediction
abstract: Motivation: Plant disease resistance genes, particularly those encoding NB-LRR proteins, are important targets for crop improvement. Proteome-based domain or motif searches can only identify NB-LRRs among existing gene models, meaning they cannot recover loci that have been missed or incorrectly predicted by the reference annotation. The full-length, homology-based R-gene prediction (HRP) method circumvents this issue by reconstructing gene models directly on the genome. However, the original implementation of this method requires several separate phases of classification, comparison and filtering operations. Results: HRPv2 is an automated, enhanced version of the original strategy. The labour-intensive, step-by-step curation process used in HRP has been replaced by a reproducible filtering framework. Enhancing two steps of the homology search process has enabled HRPv2 to better account for the specific NB-LRR variability of the genome. Performance validation confirmed that the number of full-length NB-LRRs annotated in both the automatically predicted gene set of the respective genome assembly and the final NB-LRR repertoire has increased in HRPv2 compared to HRP. Availability and implementation: HRPv2 and its associated documentation and reproducible test data are available at https://github.com/AndolfoG/HRPv2. Detailed installation and dependency information is provided in the repository README. A version-pinned Conda package has also been developed and locally validated to provide a reproducible execution environment.
authors: Giuseppe Andolfo; Thomas Holzweber; Juliane C. Dohm et al.

title: An Exploratory Multiome Analysis of a BCG-Associated HSPC Signature: Trained-Immunity Marker in Blood and an Adverse Prognostic Association in Tumour
abstract: Intravesical Bacillus Calmette--Guérin (BCG) is an established treatment for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), and recent evidence indicates that bladder BCG induces transcriptional and chromatin changes in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs). However, the joint multi-omic structure of these BCG-associated changes and its potential to define transferable molecular signatures remain less well characterized. This study performed an exploratory integrative analysis of paired single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data from two NMIBC patients sampled before and after BCG treatment.
