Following preprocessing and barcode-level integration, 653 HSPCs were analysed using Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (MOFA+) with 2,000 HSPC-specific variable genes and 25,000 variable chromatin-accessibility peaks. Of ten latent factors, Factor~1 showed the strongest association with BCG status ($r=0.495$) and captured variation across both molecular views. RNA weights from Factor~1 were used to derive candidate gene signatures that showed partial consistency across patient-specific models. Cross-context evaluation showed associations with overall survival in TCGA-BLCA and recurrence in GSE199471, while a subset of signature genes showed consistent directional changes in monocytes following BCG vaccination in GSE184241. Together, these findings identify a candidate multi-omic axis associated with BCG exposure and suggest that its derived molecular signatures exhibit context-dependent behaviour across distinct biological and clinical settings.
authors: Sadia Ruhama

title: Random Genetic Variation Links Personality to Earnings and Wealth
abstract: Personality is associated with economic outcomes, but whether these relationships are causal remains unclear. We exploit within-family variation in genetic propensity toward the Big Five generated by random genetic transmission from parents to offspring. Combining polygenic indexes from the Lifelines cohort study with 19 years of administrative tax records in the Netherlands, we find that greater genetic propensity toward emotional stability increases earnings and household wealth, while genetic propensity toward conscientiousness increases household wealth. The other three traits show no consistent pattern across outcomes and specifications. The effect of genetic propensity toward emotional stability on earnings remains positive as we progressively account for genetic propensity toward educational attainment, cognitive performance, and depression. These findings strengthen the evidence that personality causally affects earnings and wealth.
authors: Leandro Carvalho; Sjoerd van Alten; Silvia Barcellos et al.

title: TempoBridge: Source-Conditioned Flow Matching with Optimal Transport Couplings for Single-Cell Population Transitions
abstract: Destructive single-cell measurements provide unpaired population snapshots rather than observations of the same cells across conditions. Local cell states and transition requests may also be insufficient to distinguish responses across source populations. We introduce TempoBridge, a common source-conditioned transport formulation for temporal, genetic, and chemical population transitions. Source cells initialize latent transport and provide a fixed empirical population summary. The velocity field receives this summary alongside the evolving cell state, flow time, and a structured transition descriptor. Minibatch optimal transport (OT) supplies couplings only for conditional flow-matching training paths; inference requires neither target expression nor OT computation. On held-out donors, TempoBridge achieves an Energy distance of 0.129 versus 0.144 for scGen. Genetic mean-expression $L_2$ error is 2.261 versus 3.156 for scGPT-scratch under Seen 2/2. On held-out compounds, condition-averaged drug-effect correlation is 0.598 versus 0.561 for the CellFlow adapter. Temporal ablations show higher mean distributional error after removing source context, replacing optimal transport with random pairing, or replacing flow matching with static residual regression. Together, these results demonstrate the predictive utility of a common source-conditioned transport formulation across held-out donors, gene combinations, and compounds.
authors: Bowen Han; Lingbei Meng; Shihuan Luo et al.

title: Tracing model-generated DNA with position-independent watermarking
abstract: Genomic language models can write synthetic DNA that carries no record of its origin. A generation-time watermark could provide a provenance signal, if a verifier can detect it using only the DNA sequence, a key, and published detector settings, without knowing where the generated region starts, which strand it lies on, or how it was divided into six-base tokens. We embed the SynthID tournament watermark in two genomic language models, Carbon and GENERator-v2. The verifier searches both strands, every start position, and four window lengths, and corrects its decision for the whole search. In a detection cohort of 1,544 held-out prompts, it found all 3,088 marked sequences per model, unedited and after one substituted, inserted, or deleted base. For ordinary sequences, the one-sided 95% upper confidence bound on the false-positive rate was at most 0.850%; one bound for the wrong-key control reached 1.015% (Carbon, after a deletion). In a development cohort, neither model showed a detectable change in likelihood or in predefined sequence measures. Under random edits placed without reference to the detector, detection stayed complete or nearly complete up to a 2% per-base edit rate. These results show statistical detection, not biological function, secret-key security, or robustness to an editor who sees the detector.
authors: Kimon Antonios Provatas1; Christos Galanopoulos; Ilias Georgakopoulos-Soares

title: A Unified Unsupervised Framework for Genome-Wide Association Studies in Heterogeneous Populations
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have greatly advanced the discovery of genetic variants underlying complex traits and diseases. Yet in heterogeneous populations, existing GWAS strategies typically either pool all individuals under an assumption of population homogeneity or perform meta-analysis across predefined subgroups, both of which are limited when latent genetic heterogeneity attenuates subgroup-specific effects and masks true associations or subgroup labels are imprecise. Here we present UCALM, a unified unsupervised framework that infers genetically homogeneous subgroups directly from the data and integrates subgroup-specific GWAS with a novel layered meta-analysis method to capture both shared and subgroup-specific association signals. Through extensive simulations and analyses of large-scale human and livestock cohorts, including the UK Biobank ($n \approx 487{,}000$) and a heterogeneous pig cohort ($n \approx 85{,}000$), we demonstrate that UCALM substantially alleviated the mean genomic inflation across 24 UK Biobank traits to 1.17 compared with 1.43 for GLM and 1.37 for LDAK-KVIK, and further revealed 74 loci in the pig cohort that were previously obscured by conventional approaches. Our results establish a robust and broadly applicable strategy for association mapping in structured populations and improve the resolution of genetic signals across diverse species.
authors: Xiong Shen; Zhenshuang Tang; Yong Liao et al.

title: On the sensitivity to hyperparameters of a Bayesian method to infer selection signatures
abstract: Motivated by a real-life problem, namely, inferring genomic regions affected by selection, we studied some properties of a two-step method that performs this task based on the FST. This approach exhibits computational simplicity as an appealing feature. Step one involves fitting a conjugate Bayesian model to find point estimates of FST and selecting the markers to be considered in step two, where they are grouped using such estimates. Subjective priors are frequently used in this problem and large hyperparameters may be encountered; hence, there is interest in addressing their impact. Preliminary analyses suggested that, the number of markers selected in step one tends to zero when the hyperparameters have the same value and tend to infinity, or are different but tend to infinity and their difference tends to zero. Thus, we studied how hyperparameters affect the posterior mean, variance, and predictive density of allele frequencies, and the posterior distribution of FST, formally. Moreover, an empirical approach based on simulated and real data was performed. Our main findings are summarized in two theorems that set the asymptotic behavior of the method, providing a foundation to understand the aforementioned phenomena. As to the empirical studies, the groups created in the second step, the estimated posterior means and the number of selected markers showed high sensitivity to hyperparameters. Albeit the mathematical intractability of the posterior distribution of FST, our results revealed asymptotic properties explaining two features of the method that lacked a formal elucidation.
authors: Carlos A. Martinez; Ronnal E. Ortiz; Nelson A. Cruz et al.

title: Penalize the Common Trade: A Collision-Aware Layer for Learned Portfolios
abstract: Different learning systems can make nearly the same trade when they share data, objectives, or representations. The market then sees decision concentration even if the models look diverse. We call exposure to this shared direction a signal collision. A linear-impact game shows the basic externality: each allocator chooses too much common exposure because it does not bear the full price effect imposed on others. An overlap-dependent toll recovers the social choice, and a feedback model gives the exact gain at which return-responsive allocation becomes unstable. We also state the restrictive spectral conditions under which a leading eigenportfolio can reveal the collision direction. These results motivate a simple post-model layer: subtract a penalty for loading on the recent common return mode before forming the portfolio. In a frozen panel of ten liquid cross-asset ETFs, 760 completed weeks from January 2012 through July 2026, and exact self-financing costs of 10 basis points per dollar traded, this layer changes maximum drawdown from 23.6% to 14.1%, volatility from 12.6% to 10.7%, and excess-return Sharpe from 0.664 to 0.667. A volatility-matched momentum diagnostic still draws down 19.9%. Paired stationary-bootstrap uncertainty is wide: the 95% interval for drawdown improvement is $[-3.3,18.4]$ percentage points and includes zero. The result establishes a reproducible risk-control association and specifies the holdings-and-flow validation needed to attribute the common direction to AI crowding. AI-use disclosure. Generative AI tools, including OpenAI Codex, assisted manuscript preparation. For this preprint version, Codex assisted with LaTeX editing, author and venue metadata, compilation, and layout checks.
authors: Eric Benhamou; Jean-Jacques Ohana; Beatrice Guez et al.

title: Specification LASSO and a Flexible Characteristics-Based Asset Pricing Model
abstract: This paper studies a partially linear semiparametric additive model that allows for interactions among variables in high-dimensional settings. We propose the Specification LASSO (S-LASSO), a two-step method that integrates LASSO and Adaptive Group LASSO to simultaneously perform variable selection and model specification. Theoretically, we establish that S-LASSO possesses oracle properties in terms of selection consistency and asymptotic normality. Monte Carlo simulations confirm that S-LASSO outperforms existing alternatives across a variety of scenarios. Empirically, we apply S-LASSO to a characteristics-based asset pricing model, exploring the linear and nonlinear effects of asset-specific characteristics on cross-sectional returns, as well as their interactions with firm size.
authors: Chaohua Dong; Shuyi Ge; Shaoran Li et al.

title: Interpretable Allocation and Model-Predictive Rebalancing of Equity Portfolios, Tested on Real and Synthetic Markets
abstract: A live equity portfolio poses three problems: which stocks to hold, when to trade, and whether the strategy holds up beyond the observed market. We built one system for all three and tested it on 373 US equities, calibrated on 2014-2024 and traded from January 2025 to September 2026. A selection rule chose stocks by score, by a bandit, or at random, and one of seven weighting rules, four consumer-theory utilities, and three standard portfolios, set share counts under limits on budget, single-stock weight, portfolio volatility, and turnover, with each stock's preference weight a bounded score of its trend, market beta, and the market's recent direction. A model-predictive controller forecasts portfolio value with a multi-asset geometric Brownian motion and re-planned at its horizon, when the value left its forecast band, or at a drawdown stop. To probe deeper declines than the real window held, we also ran the system on simulated markets from per-asset hidden Markov generators with jumps, linked by market and sector factors. On real prices, the stocks chosen mattered more to terminal wealth than the weighting rule, and the early re-plans shrank the worst drawdown in most rule combinations against a fixed calendar without consistently raising wealth. In the deepest simulated declines, every combination, random picks included, ended above simulated SPY and the equal-weight universe in the median, even without early re-plans, so the margin came from shared parts of the system, not from stock selection or re-plan timing. A market hedge that tightened a beta cap as the market weakened cost wealth on real prices but paid off in the most sustained simulated declines, and the generator's persistent trends favored score-based selection more than the real market did, which suggests a synthetic test judges stock selection fairly only if its generator does not build in that persistence.
authors: Jeffrey D. Varner

title: Optimal portfolio and consumption under no-shorting constraints: The exploratory formulation and reinforcement learning
abstract: We develop a reinforcement-learning framework for the continuous-time optimal portfolio-consumption via utility maximization under no-shorting portfolio constraints. We adopt the exploratory formulation under entropy regularization and impose no-shorting constraint through a componentwise nonnegative conditional-mean constraint on the class of admissible randomized policies, while the sampled actions are allowed to be negative during the training. For CRRA utility, we derive the homothetic value function and the optimal Gaussian portfolio and Gibbs consumption policies under some model conditions and establish a verification theorem. These results allow compatible parameterizations in actor, critic, and $q$ functions for a constrained policy-iteration algorithm. Policy evaluation uses trajectory-based moment conditions, and policy improvement uses fitted coefficients to solve a convex quadratic program over the nonnegative orthant without requiring market coefficients as inputs. The mean constraint preserves tractable Gaussian exploration throughout parameter learning, while modal deployment converts the learned randomized policies into deterministic controls. In particular, the Gaussian mode coincides with its constrained mean and hence satisfies no-shorting constraint, and the Gibbs mode determines the deployed consumption rule.
authors: Xun Li; Xiang Yu; Fengyi Yuan et al.

title: Non-asymptotic analysis of SGLD with discontinuous stochastic gradients: a new route to portfolio CVaR minimization
abstract: Conditional-Value-at-Risk (CVaR) optimization is a fundamental tool in portfolio selection, yet its nonsmooth loss structure poses a challenge for the existing theory of stochastic gradient methods including associated Langevin algorithms. In particular, the positive-part loss and the softmax portfolio parametrization lead to stochastic gradients that need not be globally Lipschitz continuous, but rather discontinuous, where available non-convex stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) guarantees often exhibit an unfavorable exponential dependence on the problem dimension. In this article, we develop a non-asymptotic analysis of SGLD for a regularized CVaR portfolio optimization problem. We exploit the geometric structure of the CVaR objective to establish linear growth, convexity-at-infinity, and one-sided Lipschitz properties of the stochastic gradient without imposing density assumptions on the asset losses that are typical in previous works. Crucially, the constants appearing in the aforementioned structural conditions are shown to be independent of the number of assets. Moreover, we establish a convergence bound in Wasserstein-2 distance with rate $\mathcal{O}(λ^{1/4})$ and a finite-time guarantee for the expected excess risk. Our analysis, together with the dimension-independent constants in the structural conditions, leads to an excess risk bound that depends linearly on the number of assets. Numerical experiments with simulated Gaussian portfolios exhibit the predicted dimension dependence. Computational comparisons with alternative stochastic optimization methods further illustrate the practical efficiency of SGLD for the optimization problem under consideration. Finally, we extend the framework to a broader class of non-convex stochastic optimization problems with discontinuous stochastic gradients.
authors: Yan Ding; Sotirios Sabanis; Ying Zhang

title: The Generalised Kessler Syndrome and the Persian Gulf
abstract: The term Kessler syndrome was coined for a runaway orbital cascade creating a high-density debris field. The idea is generalised and applied to supply chains. An additive channel enables failures to generate further failures; a subtractive channel erodes the capacity to contain and restore. When damage outpaces repair, failure becomes irreversible and the system settles into a new state. Supplies connect the theory to its application. Stocks insulate subsystems from one another, and their exhaustion exposes dependencies. For the Persian Gulf states, restrictions on maritime supplies from spring 2026 are inadequately compensated by air and road transport alternatives. This depletes inventories unevenly across products and impairs the functioning of the logistics system itself. Throughput optimisation builds fragility everywhere; the Gulf is where it is becoming visible, with the Strait of Hormuz restriction as the trigger. Formulated as a Kelly portfolio allocation under a weakest-link payoff, the optimal strategy concentrates resources on the lagging rather than the leading inputs.
authors: Bernhard K Meister

title: Sparse Autoencoders as Implicit Diversification Regularisers for Cross-Sectional Cryptocurrency Returns
abstract: Factor models are central to asset pricing and portfolio construction, but neural factors are often difficult to interpret, and their effect on portfolio risk is unclear. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) may address both concerns by describing daily returns across many assets with only a few active features. We ask whether this sparse representation produces stable financial factors and better-diversified portfolios. We study cryptocurrency returns, use equities as a secondary test, and compare the SAE with common benchmarks in a time-ordered evaluation. We find consistently lower volatility in SAE portfolios and link this result to lower correlations among the selected assets. However, the SAE does not outperform a simple contrarian strategy on risk-adjusted return, and its factor identities are not stable across training runs. Our contribution is to show that sparse coding can support portfolio diversification, while clearly separating this risk effect from claims about alpha or stable factor identities.
authors: Weijia Han; Lisha Qu

title: Simple Portfolios that Deliver Consistent Decent Returns
abstract: Portfolio construction has been studied extensively in both academia and industry. Its applications range from pension funds and hedge funds to private savings. The academic literature centers on methodology, commonly evaluated in settings that allow short selling, leverage, and frequent trading. Industry, on the other hand, operates under real constraints, but its data and methods are proprietary and largely unpublished. Neither is directly available to the private investor. This paper is an empirical study of established portfolio construction methods in the setting of the private investor. We consider a small investable universe of liquid US ETFs, where trading is monthly and carries a cost, and neither shorting nor leverage is permitted. Portfolio construction is posed as a convex optimization problem, its inputs are estimated from public data, and every parameter is interpretable. We denote such portfolios simple. We show that simple portfolios of as few as three ETFs deliver consistent and decent returns, without tuning to the backtest period. To find them, we have developed a framework, which we share publicly, able to backtest hundreds of portfolios on a standard laptop over a twenty year period or longer. When no return forecast is made, portfolios are constructed from risk alone, using methods such as risk parity and minimum volatility, built on a statistical factor model fitted with expectation maximization. When a forecast is made, we combine the Markowitz formulation with momentum signals and ridge regression. We report what works and what each component adds, weighing its gain against its complexity and the effort it demands of the investor. The findings are supported by numerical experiments over the past two decades, and the proposed portfolios outperform the standard 60/40 allocation.
authors: Oskar Edén Wallberg; Alexander Karolin

title: Decorrelating the Advice Layer: A Calibrated Fragility Metric and Tested Mitigations for Synchronized Liquidation in Agentic Wealth Management
abstract: Conversational AI agents are turning wealth management into a continuous loop of market analysis, allocation, risk checks and execution, run for millions of clients on a handful of foundation models. We build a multi-asset agent-based model of this layer, calibrated to measured model concentration, cross-model correlation, retail turnover and 33 years of real equity returns, and ask when the layer amplifies market declines and what prevents it. The effective number of independent decision-makers is bounded however many clients the layer serves: about 2.0 at today's consumer concentration. This monoculture of views drives crowding in individual securities and sets the blast radius of a compromised model provider, but it does not drive market-wide liquidation. Index tail losses rise with the square root of agentic adoption, are 1.47-1.90 times larger under an agentic than under a periodic robo-advice architecture, and do not rise with model concentration; synchronized automation (risk overlays, drawdown cuts and attention-driven execution) drives them. A fragility index computed from aggregate flow, public returns and an impact estimate forecasts tail liquidation out of sample (hold-out R^2 of 0.56) far better than concentration or correlation measures. Decorrelating the automation, not the models, works: dispersing overlay parameters, staging execution and a participation breaker together cut tail liquidation by 63% at no measurable cost to client welfare, whereas provider diversification has no effect. Because the statistics required are sums, they can be computed across platforms under secure aggregation with differential privacy at negligible cost for realistic client populations. In historical replays, an agentic layer holding 10% of the market would have deepened the 2020 crash by about 858 basis points.
authors: Saurabh Kohli

title: Certifying Reward Alignment in Portfolio Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Financial reinforcement learning often translates an investment objective into an additive risk-adjusted reward. An agent can optimise that reward accurately yet implement a different financial preference. We develop a decision audit for terminal mean-variance equilibrium that separates reward misspecification from learning error. In a finite exogenous-state market, we bound the gain from changing one action using actor, reward and continuation-critic residuals. The certificate ignores state-constant critic offsets, accommodates convex action constraints, and has an independent-sample extension that does not require the equilibrium policy. A continuation-aware actor-critic method estimates the future-policy correction from samples. Across nine controlled markets and twenty seeds, it reduces policy distance by and one-step deviation gain by relative to a matched myopic-reward network. A separate PPO comparison tests the same reward intervention within a standard optimiser. Historical tests cross seven covariance estimators and 10, 30 and 49 US industry portfolios over 432 months: joint reward calibration preserves each fitted mean-variance target, but does not improve realised investment performance. Together, these results provide a way to quantify whether a learned decision implements its stated financial objective, separately from how well that objective performs in a backtest.
authors: Matin Tavakoli; Seyedreza Tavakoli; Faezeh Salmani et al.

title: Optimal portfolio choice under green transition timing risk
abstract: We study an investor's optimal portfolio choice problem when they account for the impact of a possible future green transition, whose timing is uncertain. We model the green transition as a discontinuity in the stock price processes, driven by a single jump process with constant intensity, in which 'green' stocks increase in value and 'brown' stocks decrease in value. The investor is ambiguous about the timing of the green transition and designs an investment strategy which is robust to this risk. The investor has constant relative risk aversion preferences over both wealth and model ambiguity, which introduce a multiplicative ambiguity penalty for power utility and an additive ambiguity penalty for log utility. We separate the problem into pre- and post-transition cases, derive the solution, and provide a verification theorem. We further show that the log utility, ambiguity-neutral, and worst-case problems are obtained as special cases of our general problem. In a case study with one green and one brown stock, we show that when the stock prices are positively correlated, an investor who is aware of transition risk increases their investment in the green stock and reduces their investment in the brown stock, compared to when they ignore the possibility of a transition. We illustrate the difference between an ambiguity-averse and a risk-averse investor, and show how an ambiguity-averse investor re-allocates their portfolio as their view on the probability of a green transition changes.
authors: Emma Kroell; Mogens Steffensen

title: Optimal collective investment under regulatory uncertainty
abstract: We study optimal collective investment subject to a Value-at-Risk (VaR)-type constraint that accounts for uncertainty about future regulatory requirements. The constraint incorporates several possible wealth thresholds and imposes a minimum weighted average probability of meeting them. We characterize the optimal terminal wealth, which combines regions of constant wealth at regulatory thresholds with Merton-type investment regions. Unlike a classical VaR constraint with only one threshold, our formulation generates protection against several thresholds. For two possible thresholds, we identify when both are protected and when protection concentrates on the larger one. Numerical results show that the regulatory constraint can substantially reshape the optimal payoff and generate large welfare losses relative to unconstrained investment when the required compliance probability is high, even the smaller wealth threshold is high, or initial capital is limited. In heterogeneous investor pools, welfare losses depend strongly on the composition of the risk aversions and the Pareto weights governing risk sharing. Losses are particularly pronounced when highly risk-averse investors dominate the pool. Moreover, investors with smaller capital contributions can bear disproportionately large shares of the total welfare loss, while larger contributors may bear less than their capital-proportional share. Thus, regulatory uncertainty not only reduces aggregate welfare but can also create substantial disparities in how its costs are distributed among investors.
authors: An Chen; Christian Laudagé; Shihao Zhu

title: Financial Context-Rich Strategy for Actor-Critic based Agents: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach for Stock Trading
abstract: In modern financial markets, more than 3/4th of the large volume trade is executed by algorithmic trading based on advanced trading strategies to attain higher precision and speed than traditional human traders. The conventional strategies focused on price-based indicators are inadequate in capturing the market dynamism arising from real-world events such as social sentiments, political instability, or sudden economic shifts. With the rise of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and data availability, there is a requirement for more efficient algorithms that can incorporate these external factors in trading strategies. DRL has shown potential in simulating real-world scenarios and in simplifying complex decision-making since DRL agents can automate the trading process i.e. executing trades in a manner comparable to human traders. They have shown reliable performance since they can update their policies based on risk and quantitative factors. In this paper, we propose a DRL approach based on partial and deep-infusion of sentimental analysis. It features distinct policy designs of actor-critic-based agents: only policy optimization (A2C & PPO) and policy optimization along with Q-learning principles (DDPG, TD3 & SAC). Our findings reveal, that the agents based on policy optimization combined with Q-learning, significantly and consistently demonstrate improved performance upon sentiment deep-infusion in profit maximization as well as risk-averse trading.
authors: Hrishikesh Singh; Aarti Sharma; Millie Pant

title: Directionally Correct Views in Portfolio Optimization
abstract: Portfolio optimization techniques often use historical data to estimate parameters for Markowitz-type or ML models. Effective allocation requires a way to align the available data with conditions expected over the investment horizon. Inspired by the Black-Litterman framework, we ask whether incorporating expert views leads to better portfolio allocations. In a simple Markowitz setting, we show that even a small amount of directionally correct information can materially improve investment decisions. We also discuss how expert views can be incorporated in end-to-end portfolio models using entropy-based ideas. Somewhat surprisingly, our empirical results indicate that simpler Markowitz-type model perform as well as an end-to-end model, once directionally correct experts are incorporated.
authors: Ojas Kumar; Sreejit Dey; Sarvesh Ravichandran Iyer et al.

title: When News Gets Old: Portfolio Allocation with Reinforcement Learning and Large Language Models
abstract: Financial news can influence investment decisions long after publication. Timely news may reach an investor before prices fully adjust, whereas older news may already be reflected in prices. We examine two ways to handle aging signals: retain them and give a portfolio policy timing information, or filter them out before portfolio selection. A fixed large language model (LLM) extracts signals from public SEC disclosures. We compare these treatments in reinforcement learning (RL) policies and LLMs that choose portfolios directly. We evaluate returns after trading costs in historical tests over 2023-2025. RL choices respond to timing information in a controlled test, but historical returns show no consistent benefit from adding it. For the LLM, filtering old news produced the highest average net return, reaching 18.43% per year when news delivery was delayed by four weeks. This exceeded the returns of all RL strategies that used news.
authors: Bolin Song; Surui Xiang

title: Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing: A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core
abstract: LLM agents that act on live Web data must combine heterogeneous evidence, remember what they have done and improve from outcomes without weakening their own safeguards. We study this problem in autonomous investing, where every action is irreversible and based on untrusted Web content. We present Steward, a multi-agent LLM system that draws the boundary of self-evolution in its type system. First, nine role-specialised agents decide jointly: four analysts read news feeds, SEC filings, macroeconomic series and market data and emit typed reports, from which a Portfolio Manager sets target positions that a protected Risk Manager audits. Second, a seven-layer shared memory, assembled by code from the system's own record, gives each decision its position context, the market narrative, calibration and the agent's past decisions. Third, the system improves itself by review: code grades every trade and forecast nightly and writes the grades into memory, and each quarter a reflector proposes prompt learnings that a deterministic gate applies reversibly and replay of recorded inputs verifies. All three operate around an invariant core of order arithmetic, risk rules and discipline-agent prompts that no self-edit can reach. In a five-month live deployment (102 trading days, 1,632 LLM calls), the system contained a 24.6% sector drawdown to a 0.3% loss; in replay of its recorded inputs, a single model given the same raw data traded more and lost 1.35 points against the market over five days where the joint design showed no significant loss, and no injected instruction was followed; and a 2015-2026 backtest shows the core alone lowering the maximum drawdown under all 50 random entry policies. The reflector traced the dominant failure to its root cause, and the gate applied a learning that the agent adopted on trigger evenings and on no control evening. Code: https://github.com/yebof/quant-agent
authors: Yebo Feng; Jingyang Dai; Liangrui Pan et al.

title: Market Regime-Based Multi-Asset Portfolio Optimization Using Nested Clustered Optimization for Tactical Asset Allocation
abstract: We investigate the interaction between market regime detection and Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) for tactical asset allocation across heterogeneous multi-asset portfolios. The central empirical question is whether conditioning the NCO pipeline, encompassing covariance estimation, hierarchical clustering, and weight allocation, on latent market states genuinely enhances risk-adjusted performance, or conversely, whether estimation uncertainty within regime-filtered sub-samples induces severe turnover and performance drag. We implement a causal rolling Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (HMM) coupled with an adaptive rebalancing mechanism that distinguishes regime shifts from portfolio weight drift. The framework is evaluated on a monthly Indonesian multi-asset universe comprising sovereign bond yields (SBN), the LQ45 equity index, spot gold (XAU/IDR), foreign exchange (CNY/IDR), and Bitcoin (BTC/IDR) across a 56-month out-of-sample period (January 2021 to August 2025). Rigorous walk-forward backtesting reveals that standard regime-agnostic NCO achieves remarkable capital preservation and risk-adjusted efficiency, delivering a 29.97% cumulative return (5.78% annualized), a maximum drawdown of only 2.18%, a Calmar ratio of 2.65, and low monthly turnover of 5.41%. In contrast, conditioning NCO on an unconstrained HMM in a small multi-asset universe amplifies parameter estimation noise and induces excessive rebalancing (47 events; 24.58% average monthly turnover), which erodes net cumulative return to 1.60% and increases drawdown to 9.99%. These findings demonstrate that without explicit transition persistence or asymmetric downside objectives, regime-switching frameworks can degrade rather than improve clustered portfolio stability, establishing crucial empirical boundaries for machine learning asset allocation.
authors: Supriadi; Bambang Siswoyo

title: Regime-Aware Interpretable Ranking for Sector Rotation
abstract: Sector rotation is a common decision in benchmark-relative portfolio management, where portfolio managers rank sectors for overweight and underweight positions. We formulate this task as ranking sector actions by expected future risk-adjusted active performance, measured with forward sector-benchmark Sharpe ratios. Such rankings should preserve temporal information, express model outputs through economically familiar signal characteristics, account for changes in signal relevance across macroeconomic environments, and capture dependencies among sectors. We propose RegimeRank, an interpretable sector-ranking model that represents fundamental and technical signals through expert-defined temporal characteristics, conditions them on learned macro factors via cross-attention, and models cross-sector dependencies through self-attention. Expected-gradient attributions identify the contributions of individual signal-transformation pairs, while macroeconomic and cross-sector attention maps provide diagnostics of the learned conditioning and relational structure. We evaluate RegimeRank on weekly S&P 500 data from 2002 to 2024 under combinatorial purged cross-validation, where it outperforms representative ranking and machine-learning baselines across multiple ranking metrics. Ablation studies support the contributions of latent macro states, regime conditioning, and cross-sector modelling, while attribution and attention analyses illustrate the temporal characteristics, macro states, and sector relationships underlying its rankings.
authors: Kelvin J. L. Koa; Ziling Liu; Xinyang Li et al.

title: Optimal Trading Filters and the Value of Predictive Signals
abstract: The value of a forecast depends on its accuracy, but also on its actionability. In trading, an investor must translate return forecasts into positions while accounting for trading costs and the lingering impact of earlier trades. We solve the stationary quadratic trading problem with transient price impact using tools from prediction theory: Wiener-Hopf factorization gives the optimal policy as the composition of a conditional forecast and an explicit causal linear filter. We recover the Gârleanu-Pedersen aim-portfolio under exponential resilience and derive fractional trading filters under power-law impact decay, requiring memory beyond finite-dimensional LQR control. At fixed positive risk penalty, signals of equal instantaneous predictive strength have equal frictionless Markowitz value. With trading costs, net attainable value is determined by the mean square of the friction-weighted conditional forecast. Under power-law impact with exposure bleeding, we find an intermediate optimal mean-reversion rate for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck signals.
authors: Matteo Smerlak

title: Rachev-Ratio Portfolio Optimization with TimeGAN Scenarios: Replacement versus Supplementation
abstract: This study evaluates the reliability and investment consequences of scenarios from a specified time-series generative adversarial network (TimeGAN) in Rachev-ratio portfolio allocation. Using 12 exchange-traded funds, we compare historical, replacement and hybrid policies across five training seeds with delayed execution and transaction costs. Synthetic probability mass varies independently of draw count under a fixed training protocol; optimal generator fidelity is not assumed. Generated scenarios understate volatility and tail losses and distort dependence. Limited longer-training diagnostics improve reconstruction loss without improving cross-asset correlation accuracy. Higher-mass hybrids earn larger average net returns in some configurations, but all conditional generated-versus-historical return intervals include zero at the reference block length. Full-period TimeGAN means exceed resampling controls, while direct paired return, Sharpe and realized-tail-ratio intervals include zero. Replacement raises turnover and is sensitive to the modified objective's denominator floor; changing that floor does not uniformly improve realized downside risk. Exploratory generation-error associations do not identify a causal investment-performance channel. The results illustrate financial model risk from the interaction of imperfect scenarios and a tail-sensitive allocation criterion, supporting joint evaluation of fidelity, numerical behavior and realized outcomes within the tested implementation.
authors: Yifan He

title: Dynamic portfolio selection under range value-at-risk with logarithmic returns
abstract: This paper studies continuous-time portfolio selection under Range Value-at-Risk (RVaR), with both portfolio performance and risk evaluated in terms of logarithmic returns. We formulate a mean--RVaR problem in a continuous-time financial market and reduce the dynamic optimization to a static quantile problem. Using quantile representation, Lagrangian optimization, and convexification, we characterize the optimal terminal wealth through the convex envelope of an RVaR-specific transformed weighting function. The RVaR-specific convex envelope exhibits two distinct geometric configurations. Under Scenario~1, the terminal wealth has a VaR-type structure: the minimum-RVaR payoff is digital-option-like, whereas for $0<λ<1$ it consists of two growth-optimal regions separated by a constant-payoff region. Under Scenario~2, the convex envelope is determined either by a supporting line connecting an interior contact point to the endpoint or by a common supporting line with two interior contact points, leading to a richer multi-region payoff structure. We further show that the RVaR solutions reduce to their VaR and Expected Shortfall (ES) counterparts as $β\downarrowα$ and $α=0$, respectively. Under constant investment opportunities, we also derive closed-form wealth processes and replicating portfolio strategies. Numerical results show that the effects of $(α,β,λ)$ on risky-asset exposure are nonlinear and generally non-monotone. In particular, when $α>0$, pure minimum-RVaR optimization may assign zero terminal wealth in sufficiently bad states because the extreme quantile region $[0,α)$ is excluded from the RVaR criterion. These results clarify how interval-based quantile risk control shapes state-dependent portfolio payoffs and connects RVaR with its VaR and ES limiting cases.
authors: Hui Mi; Yuzhe Pan; Zuo Quan Xu

title: From Alpha to Execution: Trading Horizons, Regimes, and Schedules under Concave Impact and Hurst Scaling
abstract: Classical execution models assume linear impact, diffusive prices, and an exogenous horizon. We study execution under concave power-law impact and Hurst-scaled price fluctuations, and make two contributions. First, we choose the execution horizon by maximizing the Sharpe ratio of the trade's realized P&L. Price moves during the execution window are part of that P&L, so executing more slowly reduces its variance, and because impact is concave it can also lower cost per share. Urgency comes only from alpha realized while the order is being worked. The problem is governed by the signs of two quantities: (i) the duration elasticity of impact $a$, which under a structural prior equals the impact-persistence gap $β- H$ and can take either sign; and (ii) the net urgency $ν$, the rate of alpha realization net of exposure relief. When $ν$ keeps its sign over the window, an interior optimum exists, to leading order in $T/t_f$, only when both are positive; otherwise the order should be worked at the fastest or slowest admissible pace. In the interior regime the first-order condition involves no impact coefficient, order size or volume, and the objective is flat: for a large-cap example, the window within 1% of maximal Sharpe spans more than an order of magnitude. Second, given the window, we derive the schedule shape by convex programming under an envelope cost. For any increasing per-share cost of delay $w(t)$, the KKT solution is $φ\propto (λ- w(t))_+^{1/β}$. For a Hurst-scaled envelope $w \propto t^H$, the normalized schedule depends only on $(β, H)$, has a closed form via the incomplete beta function, is front-loaded, and tapers smoothly to zero, saving 10-17% of envelope cost relative to a constant-rate (TWAP) schedule of equal duration. Whether it uses the whole window depends on a single dimensionless robustness level, for which we give a calibration.
authors: Dnyanesh Kulkarni; Revant Nayar

title: Reading the News Without Hindsight: NoLBERT Topics and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns
abstract: Language models that read financial news are usually trained on text from the same years used to test them, so a backtest can reward hindsight. We build news topics from NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, adapted into a sentence encoder by contrastive fine-tuning on passages of the same article, with no labels or returns. We compare it with LDA, MiniLM and FinBERT readers on 1.26 million articles from 2012 to 2024, convert each reader's topics into attention shocks and stock exposures, and forecast the returns of the 1,000 largest US stocks with eight models at three rebalancing frequencies. Models are fitted on 2013-2019, choices are made on 2020-2021, and 2022-2024 is held out. The experiment with the best validation score loses money at every frequency. Measuring attention shocks against the past 63 trading days instead of 5 raises the test rank IC of every reader. NoLBERT gives the most stable topics and forecasts about as well as LDA. An equal-weight combination of all readers and models earns a monthly net Sharpe ratio of 1.12, significant against zero before adjusting for the search but not against a price-only benchmark.
authors: Kevin Foley; Jonathan Hartadi; Shivesh Prakash et al.

title: Loss-versus-rebalancing with external proportional transaction costs
abstract: We study liquidity provision in automated market makers when trading in the external market incurs proportional transaction costs. We consider both separately collected fees and fees retained in reserves. The benchmark is a self-financing strategy holding the same total risky inventory and trading at the external bid and ask. Under continuous external prices and pure arbitrage, the pool and benchmark have identical liquidation wealth whenever the pool fee or the external spread is positive. Thus loss-versus-rebalancing relative to this transaction-cost benchmark is zero, even without a pool fee if the external spread is positive. We then construct retained-fee utility-indifference pools that implement admissible decreasing inventory schedules, and geometric mean pools that implement feasible constant no-trade boundaries for portfolio weights. These results offer an investment interpretation of liquidity provision: by choosing the pool design, a liquidity provider can specify a trading strategy whose rebalancing is carried out by arbitrageurs.
authors: Masaaki Fukasawa

title: Data-Driven Dynamic Portfolio Selection with Vine Copula Simulation and Reinforcement Learning
abstract: We develop a data-driven approach to dynamic portfolio selection that combines vine-copula simulation with reinforcement learning. The investor has constant relative risk aversion and maximises expected terminal utility with a running penalty on the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of one-period losses. We estimate a conditional vine model from historical returns and use it to generate joint scenarios for CVaR evaluation and conditional paths for training a recurrent portfolio policy. Under uniform local derivative bounds, we propagate edgewise pair-copula parameter errors through the conditional transforms to obtain power-law stability bounds in Hellinger distance and total variation. In a finite-horizon investment model, we combine these estimates with a marginal and structural approximation budget to bound policy values, optimal values and the true-market loss of policies selected under a fitted model, with separate simulation and numerical optimisation terms. On a seven-asset panel comprising US and Chinese equities and gold, the selected ensemble of ten trained policies achieves a compound annual growth rate of 34.13% and a Sharpe ratio of 2.31 over 22 complete monthly holding periods, exceeding the corresponding values of six classical and vine-based benchmarks. Combining simulated and historical training data reduces monthly target-to-target turnover by 41.5% relative to training on historical data alone, while maintaining comparable growth.
authors: Gabriël M. J. Gelissen; Fengyi Yuan

title: The Missile and the Toll: Two-Way Flow Through the Strait of Hormuz
abstract: Tolls for safe passage and attacks on shipping are usually treated as mutually exclusive: either ships pay or attacks happen. We argue they are complementary. In a Stackelberg escalation game for the Strait of Hormuz, the enforcer chooses an attack intensity and a toll schedule; the response is to pay, cross exposed, wait, reroute, or exit. Attacks create the willingness to pay; tolls harvest it. The model predicts asymmetry across trade forms: a toll where the cargo owner can pay and the vessel owner will consent, and none where either fails. Any such payment is clandestine, but the model's implications are testable against freight rates, insurance premia, and incident reports.
authors: Bernhard K Meister

title: Risk Measures for the Climate Transition Age: Why Symmetric Risk Budgets are unlikely to mitigate two-dimensionally asymmetric Climate Change risks
abstract: The most widely used investment risk measures - variance, standard deviation, and tracking error - treat upside deviations as equally undesirable as downside losses. In stable markets with assumed symmetric return distributions, this simplification is potentially harmless. In the climate transition age, it is not. Climate risk is two-dimensionally asymmetric, across assets and over time. Both dimensions are negatively skewed against investors. Hence, climate transition investment strategies deliberately deviate from benchmarks that reflect an insufficiently decarbonising global economy. When fiduciaries enforce tracking error budgets that penalise outperformance just as heavily as underperformance, they inadvertently constrain exactly the portfolio return opportunities that climate-aware investing seeks. We argue that replacing symmetric deviation-based risk measures with their downside-only counterparts - semi-variance, standard risk and trailing error - resolves this conflict without sacrificing any fiduciary discipline. The distinction is not merely semantic: as the gap between climate transition trajectories and market benchmarks widens over the coming decades, symmetric risk budgets will become binding constraints on transition strategies well before actual investment risk warrants it. We propose specific changes to mandate design that would allow institutional investors to pursue climate transition opportunities within genuinely risk-aware (rather than deviation-averse) frameworks.
authors: Lars Dijkstra; Andreas G. F. Hoepner; Fabiola I. Schneider et al.

title: Portfolio Decarbonization under Incomplete Carbon and Transition Information
abstract: We study dynamic portfolio decarbonization under incomplete information about firms' carbon intensities and the underlying transition state. The investor maximizes expected utility of terminal wealth net of a penalty on perceived cumulative financed emissions. Asset returns and carbon intensities depend on a stochastic transition factor, while the investor may need to infer the current transition state, its long-run mean and firms' carbon intensities from market observations and periodic noisy disclosures. The optimal strategy combines a Merton-type component with climate-dependent expected-return adjustments, a direct carbon intensity penalty and intertemporal hedging demands associated with stochastic carbon intensities and learning. In a numerical application, incomplete information has limited effects on welfare and target satisfaction when prior beliefs are well specified. By contrast, biased beliefs generate welfare losses in either direction but asymmetric environmental consequences: optimistic and pessimistic beliefs induce opposite portfolio tilts and therefore affect the probability of exceeding the cumulative emissions target differently.
authors: Olivier Féron; Ruben Haalebos

title: On integrability of local utility maximizing strategies
abstract: In stochastic control problems involving optimal portfolio choice, one often seeks an optimizer of some local criterion (dynamic programming value function) generated by some global criterion (e.g., expected utility). The local optimizer then typically acts as a stochastic integrand with respect to some multivariate stochastic process (e.g., asset prices). This paper takes a closer look at local criteria in the form of ``local expected utility''. Since the existence of the local optimizer can be established under very mild conditions, it is crucial to understand under what circumstances the local optimizer has good integrability properties. It is shown that the reasonable asymptotic elasticity condition of Kramkov and Schachermayer (1999) applied to the local utility function plays a key role in this context.
authors: Aleš Černý; Johannes Ruf

title: A Mean Field Model of Consumption Inertia and Keeping Up with the Joneses
abstract: Households compare their living standard with others' and dislike changing it. We study consumption and investment when felicity depends on consumption relative to a benchmark, the population's geometric average consumption, and cuts in felicity weigh more than increases. Asset returns are exogenous. For finitely many types and arbitrary initial wealth and inherited standards, a mean field equilibrium exists under a weak interaction condition, and for fixed budget multipliers the benchmark is the fixed point of a contraction. In a complete market with common risk, a mean field equilibrium at empirical type frequencies is an exact Nash equilibrium of the finite game, for any preferences over relative consumption. We bound the gain from deviating when plans computed at another composition are used. We compute equilibria in which groups with different wealth, inherited standards, and loss aversion revise spending at different dates. With identical households and common risk, the unique symmetric equilibrium is the policy of a single loss averse household with modified curvature. In a baseline example, ignoring the inherited standard costs up to 17% of wealth, while small errors about the composition of the reference group cost less than 0.5%.
authors: Junkee Jeon

title: From Economic Explanation to Performance Improvement in Machine-Learning Portfolios
abstract: To extend conventional model-level feature importance to economically meaningful portfolio outcomes and decisions, we propose a local first-order attribution-propagation framework that maps allocation-function feature exposures to local sensitivities of sequential portfolio performance metrics. We relate the propagated attributions to Shapley values defined directly for portfolio objectives and derive statistical inference for Sharpe-ratio attributions. The resulting attribution-guided feature-exposure intervention enables post-training adaptation, translating portfolio-metric explanations into out-of-sample decisions without retraining the underlying allocation model. We further introduce temporal stabilisation and cross-model averaging as complementary regularisation mechanisms. Empirically, the interventions yield statistically significant improvements in net Sharpe ratios across different model classes.
authors: Yunqi Liang; Stefan Zohren; Mihai Cucuringu

title: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery
abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.
authors: Jie Huang; Yuecheng Hong; Yao Chen et al.

title: Ex Ante and Scenario-Conditional Value of Information in Dynamic Portfolio Choice
abstract: Portfolio decisions are often made under uncertainty about expected returns, and investors revise their beliefs as new information arrives. Although richer information generally cannot reduce optimized value ex ante, the trading strategy it induces need not improve on the strategy induced by a less informative information structure in every fixed-drift scenario. We introduce scenario-conditional expected utility and value of information to evaluate strategies selected under the investor's current belief. In a finite-horizon Gaussian portfolio choice model, we compare a fixed-belief investor, a price observer, and an attentive investor who also processes an auxiliary signal under an attention capacity constraint. Ex ante, price learning and auxiliary attention are valuable, and the total value of attention increases with capacity. Scenario-conditionally, learning creates a correction benefit by reducing the initial trading-position gap relative to the full-information strategy, but also a fluctuation cost through belief revisions, so the ex ante ranking can reverse. We derive the current-belief distribution of scenario-conditional value and the associated underperformance probability, defined as the probability of negative scenario-conditional value relative to fixed-belief choice. Over sufficiently short horizons, the scenario-conditional value of learning is negative when belief error is small relative to posterior uncertainty. For a given horizon, sufficiently high attention capacity yields a higher scenario-conditional value than any fixed finite-capacity benchmark across all drift scenarios. We also derive sharp convergence rates to full-information performance under Shannon and Tsallis technologies.
authors: Tom Pohlschmidt; Shihao Zhu

title: Entropy Regularization under No-Shorting: Structure Preservation and Convexity in Dynamic Mean-Variance Portfolio Selection
abstract: This paper studies entropy regularization for the discrete-time dynamic mean--variance portfolio problem with no-shorting constraints. In the unconstrained setting, entropy regularization can be introduced without changing the basic quadratic structure of the dynamic program. Under no-shorting, this property is lost: a standard fixed-temperature formulation generally preserves convexity but no longer preserves the homogeneous Bellman structure and the associated piecewise-linear feedback form. We introduce a state-dependent temperature that is matched to the homogeneity of the original mean--variance problem. This restores the piecewise-quadratic value function and the finite-dimensional Bellman recursion. The resulting formulation, however, makes convexity depend on the continuation coefficients generated by the soft recursion. We show that negative continuation coefficients lead to loss of convexity and prove that a common sufficiently small temperature preserves the Bellman structure and convexity over the entire finite horizon. The original no-shorting solution is recovered as the temperature vanishes. We also develop a sample-based implementation for unknown return distributions. Numerical and empirical results illustrate both the structural advantage of the state-dependent temperature and the practical relevance of the convexity-preserving temperature restriction.
authors: Xinagyu Cui; Xun Li; Ziyan Li et al.

title: Weighted selection from elliptical distributions: a stochastic representation and an application to portfolio separation
abstract: We represent (weighted-)selection-elliptical distributions as an affine combination of the $q$ selection variables plus an elliptical term whose direction alone is independent. This form suffices for $q+2$ fund separation via first-order stochastic dominance, inter alia relaxing Simaan's (1993) three-fund assumptions.
authors: Nils Chr Framstad

title: SOTA: Stock Options Trading Agents Guided by Option-Implied Return Distributions
abstract: As option markets grow and AI advances, agentic systems for option trading are gaining increasing attention. Language-model-based agents can reason over contextual information such as news, but option trading presents a particularly challenging decision problem: a single stock can have thousands of contracts, and the agent must decide both which contracts to trade and how to combine them. Existing approaches often sidestep this complexity by restricting the policy to a fixed strategy structure, such as a straddle, limiting their ability to switch strategies as market conditions change. We present SOTA (Stock Options Trading Agents), an agentic trading framework for structured option-strategy selection. SOTA abstracts the large option universe into strategy-level decisions while deterministic resolvers handle portfolio implementation. We develop SOTA by post-training Qwen3.8-27B with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. SOTA is evaluated on options on nine large-cap U.S. equities and SPY against rule-based and machine-learning strategy selectors in the same trading environment. Over a six-month out-of-sample period, SOTA earns an 18.3% total return with a Sharpe ratio of 1.60 and a maximum drawdown of 8.96%. We also document an asymmetric role of news: news improves frontier-teacher trajectories, but retaining news during reinforcement learning reduces out-of-sample return from 18.3% to -2.7%.
authors: Yizhen Xie; Mengyang Liu

title: OOM-RL II: Reality Is an Oracle, Not a Debugger Provenance-Constrained Diagnosis in Continually Evolving Agent-Engineered Systems
abstract: Reality may establish that an outcome occurred without identifying which evolving procedure produced it or why. This distinction matters in production ML systems whose code, configuration, and artifacts change while external feedback accumulates. We examine it in a human-directed, agent-engineered quantitative trading system, using oracle to mean an external source of realized outcomes rather than a complete correctness specification. Across one year, the account gained and outperformed a broad market index, while annual alpha was not statistically distinguishable from zero under the main retrospective specification. Retrospectively selected subperiods include adverse relative performance and conditional candidate-level weakness under declared approximate references. Engineering records document changes during the episode, and complete recommendation-to-runtime binding is unavailable. The archive does not establish a common frozen instance or a unique cause. The case motivates an outcome--diagnosis gap: outcome evidence, evaluated-object identity, and causal explanation support distinct claims. We distinguish frozen instances, pre-specified adaptive procedures, and ad-hoc development; organize archive-relative claim identifiability and an evidence hierarchy; and propose a prospective production-binding protocol. An illustrative compatible-history example shows how factual binding can resolve a recommendation's referent without supplying its counterfactual effect. The protocol is proposed rather than prospectively validated. External feedback constrains outcome claims, while provenance and additional identification structure determine the resolution of diagnosis.
authors: Kun Liu; Liqun Chen

title: Conditional value-at-risk under reward-penalty mechanism with applications to robust portfolio management
abstract: In this paper, we present robust portfolio selection models by incorporating a reward and penalty mechanism into portfolio management. We assume that the joint distribution of the losses of the underlying risky assets in a portfolio is uncertain but lies within a multivariate distribution set. Our goal is to identify optimal portfolio allocations by minimizing the worst-case conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of portfolio loss under the reward and penalty mechanism and distribution uncertainty. Our models can also be used to investigate the problem of how to balance portfolio losses with their associated downside risk in portfolio management. We first derive an explicit closed-form expression for the worst-case CVaR under the reward-penalty mechanism, which generalizes several existing models and results regarding the worst-case CVaR, such as those studied in Jagannathan (1977), Chen et al. (2011), and Cai et al. (2024). We then apply this expression to obtain optimal portfolio allocations that minimize the worst-case CVaR under both a classical mean-covariance-based multivariate distribution set and a generalized mean-covariance-based multivariate distribution set introduced in Kang et al. (2019). Additionally, we utilize real market data to illustrate the application of the proposed models and the corresponding optimal portfolio allocations in portfolio management. Our empirical experiments show that portfolios based on the proposed models have the potential to outperform those based on several existing related models. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that incorporating downside risk into portfolio loss helps better manage risk and can achieve higher investment returns than considering either downside risk or portfolio loss alone. Moreover, our experiments reveal the trade-off between improving expected portfolio return and controlling the worst-case portfolio CVaR.
authors: Jun Cai; Tiantian Mao; Zhiqiao Song

title: Exponential investors with weakly mean-reverting prices
abstract: We investigate a continuous-time financial market where the asset price exhibits weak (sublinear) mean reversion and has a nonzero drift. Complementing earlier work on strong (superlinear) mean reversion, we show that, for an investor maximizing expected exponential utility, the certainty equivalent grows as $O(T^{2β+1})$ where $0<β<1$ is the strength of mean reversion. An explicit asymptotically optimal strategy is also given.
authors: Balazs Hoffmann; Miklos Rasonyi

title: FactorBench: A Portfolio-Aware Benchmark for Automated Factor Mining
abstract: Factor mining seeks to discover signals from financial data that predict future asset returns and guide portfolio construction. Automated factor mining now spans genetic programming, reinforcement learning, generative models, and large language model agents. Yet it remains unclear whether advances across these paradigms yield more generalizable, distinct, and economically useful financial signals. We introduce FactorBench, a portfolio-aware benchmark comparing roughly five thousand mined factors from nine automated mining methods across five equity markets. A shared data and evaluation contract supports both symbolic expressions and executable Python factors, connecting heterogeneous discovery algorithms to common signal combination and portfolio construction procedures. FactorBench traces the outputs of mining systems across three levels: factor validity, temporal generalization, and predictiveness beyond measured risk and style exposures; within- and across-method pool distinctness, including similarity to the benchmark Alpha101; and composite-signal quality and after-cost long-only and long--short portfolio performance. After systematically assessing whether advances in factor mining translate into signal quality and portfolio performance, FactorBench finds that no paradigm consistently dominates.
authors: Zhuohan Wang; Carmine Ventre

title: Robust enhanced index tracking portfolio selection under distributional uncertainty
abstract: The enhanced index tracking (EIT) portfolio selection problem aims to construct a portfolio that is expected to outperform a benchmark index. In practice, investors face uncertainty in the joint distribution of asset and index losses, as the true distribution is typically unknown and only partial information is available. Moreover, portfolio selection requires balancing the trade-off between mean loss and downside risk while targeting higher returns. Effectively modeling and managing these factors in EIT portfolio selection is therefore of both practical and research interest. To address these challenges, this paper proposes robust EIT portfolio selection models under distributional uncertainty, guided by Pareto-optimality theory. The models minimize a convex combination of worst-case mean loss and downside risk, subject to a constraint on worst-case mean return. Two uncertainty sets are considered: one assuming a known mean loss vector and covariance matrix, and a more general set with unknown moments. Closed-form solutions are derived for the former, while the latter reduces to tractable convex optimization problems. Empirical results based on real market data show that the proposed models outperform not only the tracked index but also the equally weighted portfolio, robust mean-variance models, and robust variance models in terms of out-of-sample cumulative wealth, as well as Sharpe, Sortino, and Omega ratios. Moreover, portfolios that minimize a convex combination of worst-case mean loss and downside risk consistently outperform those that minimize downside risk alone. We also provide practical guidance for selecting optimal weighting coefficients to effectively balance risk and return.
authors: Jun Cai; Zhiqiao Song

title: Cities of Signals: Compression, Separation, and the Geometry of Novelty
abstract: A cross-sectional signal is a forecast vector over $d$ assets at each date; demeaned and normalized, it is a point on a sphere. Its city is the direction of its time-averaged vector in a common target-aligned frame, a compressed summary. When is the angle between two cities a conservative estimate of the angle between the histories? For independent uniform histories, the probability that the history angle is at least the city angle tends to one when the city angle is at most 90 degrees, with an $O(T^{-1/2})$ error bound uniform in dimension. Selecting for positive average information coefficient (IC) changes the unconditional limit to $γ_q>1/2$, about 56% for 20 assets. The bound extends to independent, rotationally symmetric histories with temporal dependence; summable products of lag correlations preserve the conditional limit. A stationary ergodic theorem allows shared signal movement and identifies the population margin determining the limiting ordering. Among 266,815 positive-IC pairs in AlphaNova's Competition May 2026, the history angle is at least the city angle for 58.9% overall, 74.1% at city angles up to 90 degrees, and 1.5% beyond. These frequencies describe the observed library and do not validate the uniform null: residual agreement is mostly positive, and an empirical second-moment diagnostic cannot be matched within that null by adjusting temporal dependence alone. On the full 776-signal sample, a city angle of at least 60 degrees selects pairs with a 94.3% success rate at the same history-angle threshold, against an 85.0% base rate, and retains 72.5% of pairs. Explicit constructions show the limits of direction-only summaries, retained lengths give sharp bounds, and shared time blocks recover missing information, here only at fine resolution. Persistent positive IC confines cities and bounds their motion; convergence also requires a stable mean direction.
authors: Marc da Costa Nunes

title: Verify Claims, Not Scores: Evidence-Based Verification of Modular Agents
abstract: When developers change one component of an agent, such as its controller, a learned model or its verifier, they usually judge the change by an aggregate task score. That score cannot tell whether improvement was attainable, which component lost value, or what the agent's own checks certify. We introduce a claim-specific verification audit for modular agents that plan, act, check and refine. Instead of scoring the agent, the audit scores the evidence: each conclusion is recorded with the evidence behind it, one of four verdicts (supported, unsupported, unresolved or not evaluated) and the boundary within which it holds. Three tools supply that evidence. Oracle policies measure attainable improvement under an explicitly stated action set, so that a low value can be traced to the evaluation rather than to the environment. Replacing one component at a time with a perfect counterpart locates lost value, with null results read as unresolved whenever a downstream component could mask them. A separate test asks whether the verifier's score identifies the quantity it is read as bounding. Applied to a constrained portfolio-allocation agent in a synthetic market with known hidden regimes, the audit shows that the value of perfect regime information depends on the action set used to measure it, that the scenario generator discards most of the regime signal while better local fidelity does not improve decisions, and that the runtime verifier can be bypassed with no visible change in outcomes. The contribution is the protocol and the evidential distinctions it enforces; the empirical findings are specific to the agent and environment studied.
authors: Ali Atiah Alzahrani

title: Spouse-Protected Tontines: Household Decumulation via Neural-Network Optimization
abstract: We develop a spouse-protected tontine in which a first death changes the household state but generates no pool transfer. The same account remains attached to the household contract until extinction and funds a spouse-only continuation phase if the retiree dies first. We derive contract-level actuarial-fairness conditions and a finite-pool mortality-credit allocation rule with exact ex post budget balance. Under a homogeneous large-pool approximation, we formulate a multidimensional decumulation problem for a representative household, with withdrawal and rebalancing controls while the retiree is alive. The objective balances expected cumulative real household payments against the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) of terminal shortfalls relative to household reserve targets, without conditioning on survival to the horizon. We develop a numerical solution method for this problem based on a global-in-time neural-network parameterization of admissible control policies. We quantify policy-induced spouse-continuation costs using expected-cost and risk-loaded payment-scale loads at both representative-contract and book levels. We characterize the large-book limit of average per-contract continuation cost as the expected representative-contract cost conditional on common market information. Numerical experiments calibrated to Australia show that the spouse-only phase is a first-order and persistent household event. In these experiments, book-level diversification removes most of the representative-contract excess upper-tail cost of spouse continuation in the large-book limit, without changing expected per-contract continuation cost. A cross-country mortality comparison indicates that the prevalence and persistence of the spouse-only phase are not specific to Australia.
authors: Duy-Minh Dang; Yukan Perumal

title: Jacobian Rank Collapse in Decision-Focused Learning
abstract: Decision-focused learning (DFL) trains predictors through downstream objectives, but a different loss need not provide an independent parameter-update direction. We characterize this restriction through the predictor Jacobian, using sparse index tracking to distinguish the covariance entries read by the optimizer from the parameter directions available to learning. Rank-one Jacobians make nonzero per-example gradients collinear; a conditional spectral bound describes near-collinearity. A batch-subspace characterization and counterexamples show why these local statements imply neither common minimizers nor collinear batch updates. Experiments examine when geometry translates into decision quality. Across 38 one-parameter equity configurations, DFL gains over MSE remain below 1.8%; a 385-parameter conditional predictor also has pointwise rank one. In validation-tuned shortest-path and knapsack experiments, full-capacity SPO+ reduces mean regret by 11.6% and 10.6%, respectively; only knapsack survives correction across eight comparisons. The capacity contrast persists on fresh datasets across batch orders and training budgets. Holding expressivity fixed, invertible coordinate scaling lowers spectral effective rank and ordinary SGD gains; compensating for the scaling restores the original trajectories. Financial forward-target controls separate forecast accuracy from decision quality; a matched neural comparison finds no aggregate DFL advantage in the tested architecture. These findings distinguish local rank restrictions, coordinate-dependent optimization and predictive accuracy. Predictor geometry helps explain available learning directions, while held-out decision quality remains the test of practical benefit.
authors: Aojie Yuan; Haiyue Zhang; Zijian Su

title: Multiperiod bond portfolio optimization with transaction costs using a Markov Decision process
abstract: Bank treasury portfolios must balance yield, liquidity, and interest-rate risk across bonds of different maturities. Static allocation rules are ill-suited to this task: portfolios concentrated in long-duration securities with no dynamic adjust- ment mechanism can accumulate large mark-to-market losses and liquidity stress under rising interest rates, as illustrated by the failure of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. We develop a tractable simulation-based framework for multi-period bond port- folio optimization under interest-rate risk and proportional transaction costs. Yield-curve dynamics are modeled using the Dynamic Nelson-Siegel parameter- ization with Vector Autoregressive factor dynamics, from which we construct a time-inhomogeneous discrete-state Markov chain approximating the joint yield process across bond maturities. This chain forms the state space of a finite- horizon Markov Decision Process in which the investor maximizes expected terminal wealth subject to proportional rebalancing costs. The optimal portfolio policy is obtained by backward induction. We also quantify the approximation error introduced by truncating the transition kernel, and show that it leaves mean terminal wealth almost unchanged while substantially distorting drawdown and tail statistics.
authors: Balaji Ramachandran; Srikanth Iyer; Shashi Jain

title: Retrieval-Augmented Diffusion Modeling for Stochastic Discount Factor Portfolios
abstract: In this work, we study portfolio optimization under the stochastic discount factor (SDF) framework by learning market state representations that capture the underlying risk structures of financial data.
